title: Introduction to ethics: moral theories and applied questions
summary: A first-year course that teaches students to reason about right and wrong. It covers the main moral theories (utilitarianism, Kant, virtue ethics, social contract theory) and tests them on hard cases, global poverty, animals and AI. Students write responses, two papers and an exam.
brief: Introduction to ethics for first-year university students: a 14-week semester, each week a 75-minute lecture and a 50-minute seminar. The textbook is James Rachels and Stuart Rachels, The Elements of Moral Philosophy, with primary readings each week. Week 1, what morality is (Rachels, chapter 1). Week 2, how to argue about ethics (Anthony Weston, A Rulebook for Arguments). Week 3, cultural relativism (Rachels, chapter 2). Week 4, utilitarianism (John Stuart Mill, Utilitarianism, chapter 2; Rachels, chapters 7 and 8). Week 5, Kant (Immanuel Kant, Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals, section II; Rachels, chapters 9 and 10). Week 6, virtue ethics (Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, book II; Rachels, chapter 12). Week 7, social contract theory (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, chapters 13 to 15; Rachels, chapter 6). Week 8, the theories tested on hard cases (Judith Jarvis Thomson, "The Trolley Problem"). Weeks 9 and 10, what we owe distant strangers (Peter Singer, "Famine, Affluence, and Morality"; Thomas Nagel, "The Problem of Global Justice"). Week 11, the moral status of animals (Peter Singer, "All Animals Are Equal"; Carl Cohen, "The Case for the Use of Animals in Biomedical Research"). Week 12, who is responsible when an AI system causes harm (Andreas Matthias, "The responsibility gap"; Robert Sparrow, "Killer Robots"). Week 13, from a case to an argument: writing the final paper. Week 14, review for the exam. Students prepare the seminar discussion questions in advance. Grading: weekly reading responses of 400 to 500 words 20%, seminar participation 10%, a 1,200-word paper defending one theory, due in week 7, 20%, a 2,000-word argumentative paper on one of the applied questions, due in week 13, 25%, and a final exam 25%, with rubrics for the papers.
policies:
Attendance at seminars is expected; participation is graded on preparation and contribution, not on how often you speak. Read the assigned texts before the seminar and bring them with you.

Papers are submitted through the course site by 11:59 p.m. on the due date. Late papers lose a third of a letter grade per day unless an extension is arranged before the due date.

AI tools may be used to brainstorm or check grammar, but not to write any part of submitted work; say in a note at the end of a paper how you used them. All work follows the university's academic integrity policy.

Students who need accommodations should contact Accessibility Services and let me know in the first two weeks.

keyIdeas: Morality is the effort to guide your conduct by reason: to do what the best reasons support, and to revise when better reasons appear. Feeling that something is wrong does not by itself justify judging it wrong.
Impartiality is the second part of the minimum conception. The interests of every individual affected count equally, and your own interests, or those of people you favor, get no extra weight.
The minimum conception is a starting point, not a theory. It rules out some positions, such as pure feeling or favoritism, but leaves open whose interests count and how to weigh them.
The Baby Theresa case tests the conception. Her parents wanted to donate her organs to other infants, and the dispute turns on what interests an infant born without most of her brain has.
Good seminar questions come from a text’s claims, reasons and cases. Seminar participation is scored on preparation and contribution, not on how often you speak.

vocabulary.definition: The practice of judging and guiding conduct as right or wrong, ideally by reasons rather than feeling alone.
The view that morality is, at the least, the effort to guide your conduct by reason while giving equal weight to the interests of everyone affected.
A consideration offered in support of a judgment about what should be done, which others could in principle assess.
Treating the interests of every affected individual as counting equally, with no favorites.
What is good or bad for a being, such as avoiding suffering or having needs met.
A claim that an action, person or policy is right, wrong, good or bad.
A condition in which a baby is born without major parts of the brain, leaving the child permanently unconscious.
A question prepared from a text that invites a reasoned answer, such as a clarifying, reasons, challenge or linking question.

study.overview: This guide reviews what makes a position moral, as opposed to a mere preference, and how to test it. Rachels and Rachels, in chapter 1 of The Elements of Moral Philosophy, set out a minimum conception of morality with two parts: reason and impartial concern for the interests of everyone affected. The conception is a starting point, not a theory. It rules some positions out and leaves hard questions open. We tested it on the case of Baby Theresa, and we practiced turning a text or case into discussion questions for the seminar.

points.heading: Part one: morality is guided by reasons
points.explanation: The first part of the minimum conception says morality is the effort to guide your conduct by reason. You do what the best reasons support, and you revise your view when better reasons appear. A strong feeling that something is wrong does not by itself justify the judgment. Suppose a hypothetical student, Sam, says eating insects is wrong because it disgusts him. Disgust is a report about Sam. A reason would have to be something that could persuade someone who does not share his reaction, such as a claim that the practice harms someone. If Sam later meets a stronger argument showing his reason fails, then revising his view is part of doing morality, not a failure of it. When you assess any moral claim, ask what reason is offered and whether a stranger could be moved by it.

points.heading: Part two: impartial concern for interests
points.explanation: The second part is impartiality. The interests of every individual affected count equally, and your own interests, or those of people you favor, get no extra weight. Take a hypothetical manager, Dev, who always makes careful, well-reasoned hiring decisions but only ever considers his cousins’ interests. Dev meets part one, since he reasons, but he fails part two, because outsiders’ interests count for nothing in his reasoning. Impartiality does not mean treating everyone identically, and it does not deny that you may have special duties to family. It means no one’s interests count for less merely because they are not yours. Together, the two parts make the conception. You need both.

points.heading: What the conception settles and what it leaves open
points.explanation: The minimum conception is not a full moral theory. It excludes pure feeling and favoritism. It does not tell you whose interests count, how to weigh them against each other, or what the final verdict should be. It is also not utilitarianism. It does not say to produce the best results for the most people. It sets constraints on a good argument and leaves the verdict to further argument. The Baby Theresa case shows this. Theresa was born in Florida in 1992 with anencephaly, a condition in which most of the brain and skull do not form, and she was permanently unconscious. Her parents asked doctors to donate her vital organs to other infants who needed transplants. They asked before she was legally dead, and removing the organs would have ended her life. A court refused. She died after nine days, when her organs were no longer suitable for transplantation. To apply the conception, list reasons on each side and mark whose interests each reason appeals to: Theresa’s, the other infants’, her parents’. The dispute turns on what interests an infant born without most of her brain has. The case concerns an infant’s death, so approach it with care.

points.heading: Preparing good seminar questions
points.explanation: Seminar participation is scored on preparation and contribution, not on how often you speak. Contribution means the quality of what you say and how well you listen to others. Good questions come from a text’s claims, reasons and cases, not from facts alone. Four kinds are useful: clarifying, reasons, challenge and linking. Practice with the public case of the conjoined twins Jodie and Mary, born in Manchester, England, in 2000. Mary could survive only because Jodie’s heart and lungs supported her. Doctors said that without separation both would probably die within months. The Court of Appeal in England allowed separation; Mary died and Jodie lived. A clarifying question is: what would count as a harm to Mary? A reasons question is: which reason supports separation, and whose interests does it appeal to? A challenge is: does the reasoning let one twin’s interests count for less? A linking question is: does the minimum conception tell us anything about whose interests win? Before each seminar, prepare questions from the assigned reading, bring them with the text, and choose the one you think will best advance the discussion.

blocks.text: Read the facts of the case (3 minutes). Then fill in the two columns. In each column, write a reason and mark whose interests that reason appeals to. This case concerns the death of an infant. You may step out at any time.
The facts
Baby Theresa was born in Florida in 1992 with anencephaly, a condition in which most of the brain and skull do not form. She was permanently unconscious.
Her parents asked the doctors to donate her vital organs to other infants who needed transplants. They asked before she was legally dead. Removing the organs would have ended her life.
A court refused the request. Baby Theresa died after nine days. By then her organs were no longer suitable for transplantation.
Your two columns

columns: Reasons for allowing the organ donation
blocks.caption: For each reason, write whose interests it appeals to in brackets after it.

handouts.key:
Possible entries, in row order; other defensible reasons are acceptable.

Row 1 — For: Donation could save infants who need transplants [recipient infants’ interests in survival]. Against: Removing vital organs would end Theresa’s life [Theresa’s disputed interest in continued life].

Row 2 — For: Theresa was permanently unconscious, so donation would not cause her experienced pain or distress [Theresa’s interest in avoiding suffering]. Against: An inability to experience pain does not by itself establish that someone cannot be harmed [Theresa’s possible interests beyond conscious experience].

Row 3 — For: Donation would fulfill her parents’ wish to help other infants [parents’ interest in making a caring decision about their child]. Against: Parents’ wishes might not justify an intervention that ends their child’s life [Theresa’s interest in protection when she cannot consent].

Row 4 — For: Successful transplants could spare other families the loss of their infants [recipient families’ interests in their children’s survival]. Against: Allowing vital-organ removal before death could undermine confidence that vulnerable patients will be protected [patients’ and families’ interests in trustworthy medical care]. This is a concern requiring argument, not an established consequence of this case.

Look for reasons linked explicitly to affected parties’ interests. Students may distinguish an interest’s existence from its moral weight. Common slips: assuming Theresa could suffer consciously; treating the parents’ wishes as Theresa’s consent; assuming that more beneficiaries automatically settle the case; presenting a possible consequence as a documented fact.

handouts.title: Find the mistake

blocks.text: Below is a short answer written for this exercise by an imagined student. It misuses the minimum conception of morality. Find the mistake, then rewrite the answer so that it is correct.
The answer

The minimum conception of morality says we must always choose the act that produces the best results for the most people. So it shows that the doctors should have removed Baby Theresa's organs, and nothing is left to argue about.

items: What is the mistake?

blocks.hint: Say what is wrong in one or two sentences.

items: Rewrite the answer so that it uses the minimum conception correctly.

blocks.hint: Your corrected version.

handouts.key:
What is the mistake? The answer confuses the minimum conception with a requirement to maximize good consequences. The minimum conception requires conduct supported by reasons and impartial concern for everyone affected. It does not itself settle whether organ removal was permissible. Even utilitarianism is not simply a rule to benefit the largest number of people.

Rewrite: The minimum conception requires us to examine the reasons for and against removing Theresa’s organs and to give impartial consideration to everyone affected. Saving other infants is a substantial reason for donation. Whether it justifies ending Theresa’s life requires further argument about her interests and the moral limits on organ removal.

Look for both requirements and an acknowledgment that further argument is needed. Common slip: replacing maximization with identical treatment, or claiming that any opinion counts as a sufficient reason.

handouts.key:
The claim, and who made it: Answers depend on the discussion. Look for an accurate, identifiable claim attributed to its actual speaker. A possible claim to record, if made, is that permanent unconsciousness means Theresa could not experience suffering. Distinguish that claim from the stronger claim that she had no interests at all.

Your challenge to it: Look for a challenge that addresses the recorded claim or its supporting reason. For example, a challenge to the stronger claim would ask why lacking conscious experiences rules out an interest in continued life or bodily integrity. A challenge should identify an assumption, offer a counterexample, or request a reason. Common slip: stating disagreement without explaining what is questionable.

One sentence, agreed by your group: Look for a precise statement of the sharpest disagreement actually heard. A possible formulation, if it matches the discussion, is: We disagreed about whether Theresa’s inability to experience anything meant that ending her life could not harm her. Common slip: reporting only the broad topic, such as organ donation, rather than the competing positions.

handouts.key:
Your one-line answer: No; impartial concern requires considering everyone’s interests fairly, but further argument is needed about Theresa’s interests and whether saving other infants justifies ending her life. Accept a different conclusion if it is supported by an argument that supplies the additional premises. Common slip: treating impartial concern as an instruction to maximize benefits.

Space for your own notes during the discussion: There is no single required verdict. A defensible answer distinguishes experiential interests, such as avoiding consciously felt pain, from possible interests in continued life or bodily integrity. Permanent unconsciousness rules out consciously experienced suffering; whether it rules out every interest remains disputed. Look for reasons supporting either position and attention to the difference between having interests and having rights. Common slips: assuming that inability to express an interest proves its absence, or assuming that biological life alone settles the moral question.

study.overview: Judging a moral argument is a matter of order. First write out what is claimed and what reasons are given. Next ask whether the conclusion follows. Then ask whether the premises are true. Last, check the wording. This guide goes through those steps with Weston’s A Rulebook for Arguments in the background. Most real disagreement turns out to sit in a premise or a word, not in the logic.

points.heading: Write the argument out: premises, conclusion and hidden premises
points.explanation:
An argument offers premises as reasons for a conclusion. Words such as because, since, so and therefore show which is which. Weston’s first rules say to separate the premises from the conclusion and to set them out in a natural order. Numbered lines make this easy to do.

Example: “Zoos are prisons for innocent animals. Imprisoning the innocent is wrong. So zoos should be closed.” Set out:
P1. Zoos are prisons for innocent animals.
P2. Imprisoning the innocent is wrong.
C. Zoos should be closed.

The argument still needs a hidden premise: practices that wrongly imprison innocent beings should be stopped. A hidden premise is not a trick. It is what the conclusion needs in order to follow. To find one, ask what must be true for the stated reason to count. In “You promised to help Dan move, so you ought to go,” the missing premise is that promises ought to be kept. Once it is written down, you can see exactly what you would be agreeing to.

points.heading: Valid is not the same as sound
points.explanation:
An argument is valid if the conclusion must be true when the premises are true. Test it by supposing the premises are true and asking whether the conclusion could still be false. If it could, the argument is invalid. A sound argument is valid and has premises that are in fact true. Validity concerns the form of the argument, so it never shows that the conclusion is true.

There are three kinds of argument. A sound argument is valid with all premises true, so its conclusion must be true. A valid but unsound argument is valid with at least one false premise, so its conclusion may be true or false. An invalid argument is one where the conclusion could fail even if the premises hold, so the premises do not guarantee it, though they may still give it some support.

Example X: “All acts that cause pain are wrong. Vaccination causes pain. So vaccination is wrong.” This is valid, because if both premises were true the conclusion would follow. But P1 is false, since causing pain is not enough to make an act wrong. So X is valid but unsound.

Example Y: “Anyone who steals acts wrongly. Mara acted wrongly. So Mara stole.” The premises are plausible, but the argument is invalid. Someone can act wrongly without stealing.

A common slip is to say “it is valid, so the conclusion is true.” Say instead that the argument is valid, and that whether it is sound depends on whether its premises are true.

points.heading: Name the premise you reject
points.explanation:
Most moral disagreement is not about logic. It is about whether a premise is true. Saying “I reject the conclusion” gives the other person nothing to work with. Saying “I reject P1, because...” starts a real argument.

Example: “Any act that breaks a promise is wrong. Ben broke a promise to meet Ana so that he could save a stranger’s life. So Ben acted wrongly.” The argument is valid. Someone who thinks Ben acted rightly cannot fault the form. They should name P1 and say why it is doubtful: a promise to a friend may give way when a life is at stake. Now the dispute is about when promises may be set aside, and that is the question worth arguing.

When you test an argument, check in this order: conclusion, premises, validity, truth of the premises, wording.

points.heading: Loaded language and vague terms
points.explanation:
Weston’s rules for short arguments say to avoid loaded language, to use terms consistently and to give each term one meaning. A loaded word brings in a feeling or a verdict in place of a reason. A vague term leaves unclear what it applies to. Using one word in two senses is a separate fault, because the argument then seems to prove more than it does.

Example of a loaded sentence: “Only a heartless landlord would raise the rent on struggling families.” The word “heartless” attacks the landlord’s character instead of giving a reason. The word “struggling” is vague: struggling to pay for what? A more concrete version is that a landlord raises rents for tenants who already cannot afford basic necessities, if that is what the speaker means. Now there is a claim that can be examined.

Example of a vague term: “Unnatural behavior is wrong. Cloning is unnatural. So cloning is wrong.” If “unnatural” means not found in nature, P1 is false, since much of medicine is not found in nature. If it means contrary to human good, then P2 must be argued and cannot just be assumed.

Neutral wording is not weaker wording. The reason has to be stated instead of implied. Revising an argument does not settle the moral question. It shows what the real disagreement is, so that it can be argued.

The four arguments

items: Cruelty to animals is wrong; boiling a live lobster is cruelty; so it is wrong.
Every wrong act is punished by law; tax evasion is punished by law; so tax evasion is wrong.
Only a heartless person would let the poor go hungry, so the city must pass the food-aid bill.
It is wrong to do what is unnatural; eyeglasses are unnatural, since nature did not make them; so wearing them is wrong.

handouts.key:
The four arguments

1. Lobster: P1: Cruelty to animals is wrong. P2: Boiling a live lobster is cruelty. C: Boiling a live lobster is wrong. Valid: if both premises are true, the conclusion must be true. Soundness requires defending both premises. For P2, look for reasons about the capacity to suffer and what makes treatment cruel. Common slip: treating the validity of the argument as proof that lobsters suffer.

2. Tax evasion: P1: Every wrong act is punished by law. P2: Tax evasion is punished by law. C: Tax evasion is wrong. Invalid: being punished by law does not establish that an act is wrong, even if every wrong act were punished. The form is: all W are P; T is P; therefore T is W. P1 is also false: betraying a friend's confidence can be wrong without being punished by law. Common slip: accepting the inference because the conclusion seems true.

3. Food-aid bill: C: The city must pass the food-aid bill. The stated reason attacks the character of anyone who would let poor people go hungry. Look for identification of 'heartless' as loaded language and recognition that the argument needs reasons connecting this particular bill to preventing hunger. A defensible reconstruction would need evidence that the bill would reduce hunger and a moral premise explaining why the city ought to adopt it. Common slip: replacing 'heartless' with a neutral adjective while leaving the missing reasons unstated.

4. Eyeglasses: P1: It is wrong to do what is unnatural. P2: Wearing eyeglasses is unnatural because nature did not make them. C: Wearing eyeglasses is wrong. If 'unnatural' consistently means not made by nature, the argument is valid, but P1 needs defense: human manufacture alone does not establish wrongness. If 'unnatural' means contrary to human good in P1 but not made by nature in P2, the argument equivocates and is invalid. Common slip: treating artificial origin as sufficient evidence of moral wrongness.

Notes for when another group leads

A claim I would take up: Answers depend on the discussion heard. Look for a specific, accurately represented claim and an indication of what the student would examine or develop. Example: 'The group said that the lobster argument is valid; I would ask what evidence supports its second premise.' Common slip: recording only a topic, such as 'animals.'

A challenge I would bring to a claim or reason: Answers depend on the discussion heard. Look for a challenge directed at an identifiable premise, inference, definition, or supporting reason. Example: 'The group treated punishment as proof of wrongdoing. Could an unjust law punish conduct that is morally permissible?' Common slip: expressing disagreement without identifying what is disputed or giving a reason.

Cultural relativism, as Rachels sets it out: 1. Different societies have different moral codes.
2. No objective standard could show one society’s code to be better than another’s.

Each student reads the four problems printed with the brief.

segments.description:
The next group on the rota sits in the middle and leads.
Each member in turn presents their chosen question for about four minutes, invites responses, keeps the talk on reasons and states where the group stands.

segments.teacherNotes: Contribution is judged by quality and listening, not volume. Items and answers: 1. Society A eats beef; society B never does, believing a cow may hold a dead relative’s soul. Do they disagree about a basic value? Not necessarily. If both societies reject harming relatives, their different beliefs about cows could explain the different practices. Society A’s underlying values are not specified. 2. A relativist says we should be tolerant because every code is as good as ours. What follows if tolerance is part of only some codes? An intolerant society is then right to be intolerant, so relativism cannot ground a duty of tolerance for all. 3. In 1850 a reformer in a slaveholding society condemns slavery. Is she mistaken by the relativist’s test? Yes, by her society’s code; progress becomes mere change, unless the relativist bites the bullet. 4. People once disagreed about the shape of the Earth. What must a relativist add to apply this to morality? A reason that moral disagreement differs, such as that nothing can settle it. Reply: the minimum conception asks us to weigh moral reasons, but whether those reasons establish objective moral truth still needs argument.

segments.teacherNotes: Expected: no. A failed argument leaves the question open. Objectivity needs its own support, and the consequences count against relativism without refuting it. Board: the argument, why it fails, three consequences, what to keep: caution about our own preferences.

Students are told that later in the course they will examine Mill’s greatest happiness principle, his distinction between higher and lower pleasures, and the main objections about justice and rights.

keyIdeas: The cultural differences argument moves from a fact about belief (the Greeks and the Callatians hold opposite views about eating the dead) to a claim about truth (there is no objective right or wrong here). Reconstructed in numbered premises, the step between them is plain to see.

The conclusion does not follow. People have disagreed about the shape of the Earth, and that never showed there was no fact about it. Some moral disagreement also comes from shared values combined with different beliefs about the facts.
Showing that an argument fails does not show that its conclusion is false. Cultural relativism needs other arguments against it, or other arguments for it.

Rachels names three consequences of taking relativism seriously: we could not call another society’s customs inferior, we could not criticize our own society’s code, and moral progress would be doubtful. Each has to be weighed, not just announced.
Relativism leaves a lesson worth keeping: be wary of treating the preferences of your own culture as a universal standard.

study.overview: Cultural relativism says right and wrong are only matters of what a society’s code holds. The most common argument for it starts from a fact: societies disagree. This guide reconstructs that argument, shows where it breaks, explains what its failure does and does not tell us, and sets out three consequences Rachels says we must face if we take relativism seriously. It follows James Rachels and Stuart Rachels, The Elements of Moral Philosophy, chapter 2.

points.heading: The cultural differences argument in numbered premises
points.explanation: Herodotus tells the story in the Histories, book 3. King Darius asked some Greeks what payment would make them eat their dead fathers. They refused at any price, because the Greeks burn their dead. He then asked the Callatians, who eat their dead as a mark of honor, whether they would burn them. They were horrified. Each people finds the other’s custom an outrage. A relativist wants to use this to show that there is no objective right or wrong about the matter. Written out, the argument runs: 1. The Greeks believe eating the dead is wrong. 2. The Callatians believe eating the dead is right. 3. Therefore eating the dead is neither objectively right nor wrong; it is only a matter of what a people believes. Both premises are about what people believe. The conclusion is about what is true. Putting the argument in numbered steps makes that change of subject easy to see. Do not confuse the argument with the claim that cultures differ. That claim is true and nobody disputes it. Relativism says much more: that no objective standard could rank one code above another, and that right and wrong are only what a society’s code holds.

points.heading: Why the conclusion does not follow
points.explanation: The argument needs a hidden premise: if people disagree about whether X, there is no objective truth about X. Test that premise on another case. Some peoples have disagreed about the shape of the Earth. If the hidden premise were true, there would be no objective truth about its shape. But there is a fact about it, whatever people have believed. So the form of the argument can lead from true premises to a false conclusion, and the form is unreliable. There is a second problem. The Greeks and the Callatians may share a value, respect for the dead, and differ only in what they believe honors the dead. Their disagreement would then be about how to carry out a shared value, not about the value itself. Some moral disagreement is a disagreement about facts or beliefs, not about basic values. Be careful about what this achieves. It removes one argument for relativism. It does not yet show that relativism is false. A relativist might reply that moral disagreement is different in kind from disagreement about the Earth. That reply needs its own defense.

points.heading: A failed argument does not make its conclusion false
points.explanation: Bad reasoning can end in a true conclusion. Suppose a student argues: Paris is in France because Paris has a famous tower. The reasoning is poor, since many cities with famous towers are elsewhere, yet Paris is in France. So when you show that the cultural differences argument fails, you have shown only that it gives us no good reason to accept its conclusion. You have not shown that the conclusion is false. To settle whether cultural relativism is true, we need other arguments, either for it or against it. This is a habit worth keeping in your reading responses and papers. First say what the argument claims and where the step breaks. Then say what is left standing and what still has to be shown. Do not write as if refuting one argument for a view refutes the view.

points.heading: Three consequences of taking relativism seriously
points.explanation: Rachels says that if we accept relativism, three things follow. 1. We could not say that another society’s customs are morally inferior to our own. 2. We could not criticize our own society’s code, because to decide what is right we would only consult that code. 3. The idea of moral progress would be doubtful, since reform would mean only departing from the code. Suppose a society’s code says that members of one caste may not draw water from the village well, and a reformer argues that the rule is wrong. By the relativist’s test, the code is the standard, so the reformer is departing from it. Her campaign looks like a change, not an improvement. Each consequence has to be weighed, not just announced. A relativist might accept the first as a healthy check on arrogance. The second and third are harder: can she still say that the reformer improved anything? Rachels treats these as costs. Your task is to decide how heavy each cost is and to give a reason. Relativism also leaves one lesson worth keeping: be wary of treating the preferences of your own culture as a universal standard.

Reason: A relativist can maintain that a society's code supplies the standard of rightness, even when individuals reject it.

The idea of moral progress would be called into doubt.

1. Not necessarily. The societies may share a prohibition on harming relatives but disagree about whether cows contain relatives' souls. Different factual or religious beliefs could explain their different practices. Society A's underlying values are unspecified, so shared values are a possibility, not an established fact. study.overview: Mill’s utilitarianism gives one test for right action: does the act tend to promote happiness, with everyone’s happiness counted equally? This guide covers the principle, what it takes to apply it, Mill’s claim that pleasures differ in quality, and the strongest objection, that utilitarianism cannot respect justice and rights. Use it to check that you can state each idea in your own words and test it on a case.

points.heading: The principle of utility
points.explanation:
Mill (Utilitarianism, ch. 2 (to confirm)) holds that an act is right to the extent that it tends to promote happiness, and wrong to the extent that it tends to produce the reverse. Happiness means pleasure and the absence of pain. Rachels (ch. 7 (to confirm)) draws out three ideas: only consequences matter, only happiness counts, and everyone’s happiness counts equally. Consequences are the results of the act, not the agent’s motive. The principle is not about the agent’s own pleasure. It counts everyone affected, and it asks the agent to be impartial between their own happiness and a stranger’s.

Example: suppose a city (a made-up case) can fund only one project. A flood wall would protect 300 homes on a riverbank that floods every few years. A new park would give 30,000 residents a pleasant place to walk. The principle does not name the winner. It tells you what to ask: which choice produces more happiness across everyone affected, each person counted once? Whoever makes the decision gets no extra weight.

points.heading: Applying the principle needs a hidden premise
points.explanation:
A utilitarian argument about a real choice has premises about outcomes, and it also relies on a premise about how to weigh unlike goods. Reconstruct the flood wall argument:
1. An act is right if it produces the most happiness for everyone affected, each counted equally.
2. Suppose the suffering prevented by protecting the 300 homes is severe and lasting, while the park gives each of its 30,000 users a small pleasure.
3. The severe harm to 300 people outweighs the small pleasures of 30,000.
4. So the city should fund the wall.

Premise 3 is the one people leave unstated. The principle says to maximize happiness, but it does not say how to trade severe harm to a few against mild pleasure to many. Someone who chose the park may reject premise 3. Their disagreement is then about weighing, not about the principle. When you write or assess an argument, find this kind of premise and ask whether it is defended.

points.heading: Higher and lower pleasures
points.explanation:
Critics charged that a theory built on pleasure suits pigs. Mill replied that pleasures differ in quality as well as amount. Lower pleasures are pleasures of mere sensation, which humans share with animals. Higher pleasures are those of intellect, imagination and moral feeling, which use distinctly human faculties.

Mill’s test asks people who have experienced both pleasures which they prefer. If nearly all of them decisively prefer one, even at the cost of more discontent, it is the higher pleasure. This is the point of his line, which you should paraphrase rather than quote from memory, that it is better to be a dissatisfied human than a satisfied pig.

Example: suppose nearly everyone who has enjoyed both a long hot bath and the moment of finally understanding a hard geometry proof would give up the bath for the proof, even though the proof was frustrating. On Mill’s test, the proof is the higher pleasure.

Higher pleasures count for more in the sum of happiness. They are not thereby morally required. Critics say the test is circular, because the judges may count as competent only if they share Mill’s tastes. They also say it is elitist. Be ready to state one of these objections and say whether Mill can answer it.

points.heading: The objection from justice and rights, and the replies
points.explanation:
Rachels (ch. 8 (to confirm)) presents the objection that utilitarianism would sometimes approve acts that violate justice or rights. Consider a made-up case. A sheriff knows a violent mob will riot unless someone is convicted of a crime that has just been committed. The real culprit cannot be found. The sheriff could frame an innocent stranger passing through town. The riot would kill five people, the stranger would be executed, and no one would ever learn the truth. Suppose also that, counting every consequence, framing him produces more happiness than refusing. An act utilitarian, who judges each act by its own consequences, must then approve the framing. The objector says that verdict is wrong, so the principle is wrong.

There are three main replies, and each has a cost.
- Count all the consequences. Lost trust in the courts and fear that anyone could be next may make framing him worse overall. But this denies the case as stipulated. It works only if those real effects outweigh preventing the riot.
- Rule utilitarianism. Judge acts by the rules whose general acceptance would produce the most happiness, such as never punishing the innocent. But if you break the rule when breaking it would produce more happiness, the theory collapses into act utilitarianism. If you keep the rule anyway, you seem to follow a rule against its own aim.
- Ground rights in utility. Mill does this in a later chapter (ch. 5 (to confirm), not assigned). The cost is that a right then depends on happiness and cannot stand against it.

A reply that simply says the stranger has a right not to be punished, and that no gain in happiness can override it, is not open to a utilitarian unless that right is grounded in utility. When you assess a reply, ask what it gives up.

blocks.text: Read the four problems below. Then reread the discussion questions you prepared from Mill, Utilitarianism, chapter 2, and Rachels, chapters 7 and 8, and choose the one you think will best advance discussion of the reading.
Problems for this meeting

items: Mill says competent judges who know two pleasures prefer the higher one. Suppose nearly all judges who have tried both prefer reading philosophy to idle scrolling. Does that show the first is higher in quality, or only that judges like it?

Suppose, in a hypothetical case, a surgeon has five patients, each needing a different organ, and a healthy visitor whose organs match all five. No one would ever find out. Suppose also that, counting every consequence, the transplants produce more happiness overall than refusing. What must an act utilitarian say, and what does the case show?

A rule utilitarian follows the rules whose general acceptance would maximize happiness, such as never punishing the innocent. Suppose breaking the rule in one case would produce far more happiness. Follow the rule or break it?
Mill asks each person to be as impartial between their own happiness and a stranger's as a disinterested observer. Does this clash with a parent's duty to their own child?

handouts.key:
1. Higher and lower pleasures. On Mill’s account, a settled preference among people adequately acquainted with both pleasures provides evidence of higher quality. The judges must be able to appreciate both; mere exposure is insufficient. Their preference should concern the pleasure itself, independently of a sense of moral obligation (Utilitarianism, chapter 2). Look for an explanation of why informed preference might establish quality, followed by an objection about how judges are selected or whether preference establishes anything beyond taste. The hypothetical preference for philosophy supports Mill’s conclusion only if these conditions hold. Common slip: assuming that philosophy is automatically higher because it is intellectual, or that any majority preference establishes higher quality.

2. The surgeon. Given the stipulated consequences, an act utilitarian must approve killing the visitor and distributing the organs. Saving five lives alone does not establish this verdict; the decisive stipulation is that the act produces more happiness overall after every consequence is counted. The objection is that this verdict permits killing an innocent person and violating that person’s rights. Look for the argument: act utilitarianism approves the killing; the killing is morally wrong; therefore, act utilitarianism gives an incorrect verdict. The conclusion depends on defending the second premise. Common slip: invoking discovery or reduced trust in hospitals when the hypothetical rules out their reversing the balance of happiness. Rule utilitarianism offers a different response by assessing rules through their general acceptance.

3. Rules and exceptions. A rule utilitarian can maintain that the justified rule should be followed even when breaking it would maximize happiness in this particular case. The justification concerns the consequences of general acceptance of the rule. An exception is permissible if it belongs to the best justified rule, rather than merely because this act has better consequences. Look for the tension between fidelity to a utility-justified rule and maximizing utility in an individual case. Critics describe strict adherence as rule worship; allowing every utility-increasing exception threatens collapse into act utilitarianism. Neither objection establishes without further argument that every form of rule utilitarianism fails. Common slip: treating the consequences of one violation as identical to the consequences of general acceptance of a rule permitting such violations.

4. Parents and impartiality. Impartiality gives a parent’s child’s happiness the same moral weight as a stranger’s comparable happiness. It does not require parents to perform identical actions toward every child. A utilitarian can defend parental partiality through its benefits: parents often have special knowledge, sustained relationships, and effective opportunities to care for their children. The harder case arises when favoring one’s child produces less happiness overall than helping strangers. An act utilitarian must then favor the act with better overall consequences. Look for a distinction between equal consideration of interests and identical treatment, and between an outcome-based defense of parental duties and a duty grounded in the relationship itself. Common slip: assuming either that utilitarianism forbids all parental partiality or that its justification of ordinary parental care settles every conflict.

Selection of a discussion question: no single question is required. Look for a question grounded in the assigned reading that identifies a substantive interpretive issue, disputed premise, or objection and invites reasoned responses.

The teacher explains the format: students lead, the teacher listens and scores as it happens, and gives a synthesis at the end. Students sit in their groups of four.

segments.title: Choose your questions
segments.description:
Each student reads the four problems printed with the brief.
Each student rereads the discussion questions they prepared from Kant, section II, and Rachels, chapters 9 and 10, and chooses the one they think will best advance discussion of the reading.
The teacher walks round and notes who has questions written.
segments.teacherNotes:
Questions are the student’s own; do not supply or correct them. Students use their own copies of Kant and Rachels.
Problems printed with the brief, and answers:
1. In Groundwork section II, Kant gives four examples. One is a prosperous person who decides to give nothing to others in need. Can this maxim be universalized without contradiction? Kant says it still fails. How does its failure differ from that of the false promise? Answer: a world where no one helps could exist, so there is no contradiction in conception. But a rational agent could not will it, since he will sometimes need help. This is a contradiction in will. The false promise fails already at conception, because promising would not exist.
2. Suppose, in a hypothetical case, a recruiter tells applicants a position is paid when it is unpaid, to get free work. Another recruiter honestly offers a low-paid job that applicants may refuse. On the humanity formula, which treats the applicants merely as means, and what does consent have to do with it? Answer: the first. Deception means they cannot agree to the real terms. The second uses their labor but treats them as agents who may refuse. Critics ask how far consent goes under pressure.
3. Suppose one person’s maxim is ‘I will lie whenever it suits me’ and another’s is ‘I will lie to a murderer to save an innocent life’. The first fails the universal law test. Does the second? Does the result show that the test depends on how the maxim is described? Answer: the second requires a separate argument. Ask whether a universal practice of lying to murderers would defeat the protective purpose of this maxim, and whether the maxim could be rationally willed. The survival of general trust alone does not settle either question. Critics say the test can be tuned by description. A Kantian needs a rule for describing maxims, using the agent’s real reason without trimming it to fit a verdict.
4. Mill and Kant both say lying is normally wrong. Suppose, in a hypothetical case, a lie would save a friend from a murderer. Is their disagreement about the facts of what a lie would cause, or about something else? Answer: not the facts, since both can agree the lie saves the friend. They disagree on whether the wrongness of lying depends on results. Kant says no. Mill says yes, so the lie is permitted. A Kantian may add that one can stay silent or refuse to answer.

One student from each group reports its sharpest disagreement in one sentence.
Everyone writes a one-line answer to this question: does Kant’s verdict on lying to the murderer count against his theory, or only against the view that duties admit no exceptions? Why?

keyIdeas: Kant locates moral worth in acting from duty, not merely in accordance with it, and he holds that moral commands are categorical imperatives that bind whatever we happen to want.

The universal law formula tests a maxim by asking whether it could be willed as a law for everyone. A promise made with no intention of keeping it fails because promising would collapse if everyone made such promises.

The humanity formula forbids treating persons merely as means. A false promise uses the lender merely as a means because he is deceived into serving a purpose he could not share. Ordinary cooperation that people agree to is not forbidden.

Kant and Mill reach opposite verdicts on lying to a murderer. Kant treats the duty not to lie as admitting no exceptions, while Mill lets truthfulness give way when a lie prevents serious harm. Their disagreement is about whether results decide, not about the facts of the case.

A command that binds only if you want a certain end: ‘If you want X, do Y’.
A command that binds every rational agent whatever they want, which for Kant is the form of every moral requirement.
Kant’s test: act only on a maxim you could at the same time will to be a universal law.
Kant’s test: treat humanity, in yourself and in others, always as an end and never merely as a means.
A being with its own aims and dignity, whose worth is not just its usefulness to others.
The failure of a maxim that defeats itself when universalized, as when promising would collapse if everyone made false promises.

study.overview: Kant asks what makes an act morally right, and his answer does not depend on results. This guide covers four ideas from Groundwork, section II, and Rachels, chapters 9 and 10: acting from duty, the universal law formula, the humanity formula, and the disagreement with Mill over lying to a murderer. The first three are Kant’s tools. The fourth shows how those tools lead to verdicts that differ from a utilitarian’s.

points.heading: Acting from duty and the categorical imperative
points.explanation: Kant separates acting in accordance with duty from acting from duty. Both can produce the same behavior, but only the second has moral worth. Take two shopkeepers who each give an inexperienced customer the correct change. The first does it because honest dealing is good for business. The second does it because she believes it is the right thing to do. Both do what duty requires, but only the second acts from duty. Acting from duty does not mean feeling nothing. It means that the motive that moves you is that the act is right. Kant also says moral commands are categorical imperatives. A hypothetical imperative has the form ‘If you want X, do Y’ and binds only if you want X. ‘If you want to pass your driving test, practice parking’ is hypothetical. A categorical imperative has the form ‘Do Y’ and binds whatever you want. ‘Do not cheat’ is meant to bind even someone who gains by cheating. Mill, whom we studied last time, held that motive does not change whether an act is right (Utilitarianism, chapter 2). Kant gives motive a central place in moral worth.

points.heading: The universal law formula and the false promise
points.explanation: The universal law formula, in paraphrase, says: act only on a maxim that you could at the same time will to become a universal law. A maxim is the rule behind an act, including its situation and purpose. A useful form is: ‘When I am in [situation], I will [action], in order to [purpose].’ The test has three steps. State your maxim. Imagine everyone acts on it. Ask whether the maxim still works and whether you could will it. Apply this to a borrower: ‘When I need money, I will promise to repay it, though I know I cannot, in order to get a loan.’ If everyone in need made such promises, no one would believe a promise of repayment, and no one would lend on one. The maxim destroys the practice of promising that it relies on. Kant calls this a contradiction in conception. By contrast, take ‘When a stranger asks for directions I know, I will give accurate directions, in order to help them reach their destination.’ If everyone did this, the purpose would not be defeated, and the maxim can be rationally willed, so it passes. A common mistake is to say the false promise fails because the world would be worse. That is a consequentialist reason, not Kant’s. His test asks whether the maxim defeats itself when universalized. Note also that how you describe a maxim matters. The test is only as reliable as the description you feed into it, and critics press this point.

points.heading: The humanity formula: persons as ends
points.explanation: The humanity formula, in paraphrase, says: treat humanity, in your own person or in another, always as an end and never merely as a means. Persons are ends because they set their own aims and have dignity, not a price. The formula does not forbid using people. It forbids using them merely as means. Paying a cashier to scan your groceries uses her work, but she agrees to the exchange and has her own purposes in it, so she is not used merely as a means. Now return to the false promise. The lender hands over money only because he is deceived about whether he will be repaid. He could not share the borrower’s real purpose if he knew it. The borrower bypasses his rational agency and steers him like a tool. That is what it means to treat him merely as a means. The idea of consent is the key. Ask whether the person could agree to what is being done to them, given the truth. Rachels develops this in chapter 10 (to confirm).

points.heading: Kant and Mill on lying to a murderer
points.explanation: Suppose a murderer comes to your door and asks where your friend is hiding. You know. If you tell the truth, he will kill your friend. A lie would send him away. Kant, in his essay ‘On a Supposed Right to Lie from Philanthropy’ (discussed in Rachels, chapter 9 (to confirm)), treats the duty not to lie as admitting no exceptions. Lying is wrong whatever the result. Mill agrees that truthfulness is very useful and that lying is normally wrong. But in Utilitarianism, chapter 2, he lets truthfulness give way when a lie prevents serious harm, so the lie that saves a life is permitted. The two do not disagree about the facts. Both can accept that the lie would save the friend. They disagree about whether the rightness of an act depends on its results. Kant says no. Mill says yes. Whether the universal law test itself forbids this lie depends on how the maxim is described, which is why the objections to Kant concern both the description of maxims and whether duties can ever admit exceptions. Allowing genuine conflicts between duties would revise Kant’s position, because he denies that duties can genuinely conflict.

handouts.key:
The form: Each maxim should identify a situation, an action, and a purpose. Assess the student's actual reason for acting, rather than a rule tailored to secure a preferred verdict.

A maxim you think passes: A suitable example is: When a stranger asks for directions that I know, I will give accurate directions in order to help that person reach the destination. Other defensible maxims are acceptable.

Universal law test for the passing maxim: If everyone acted on this maxim, accurate directions could still help people reach their destinations. The maxim does not undermine the practice it depends on, and a rational agent can will such assistance as a universal practice. Look for both a coherent universal practice and a reason it can be rationally willed. Common slip: saying only that the action produces good results.

A maxim you think fails: A suitable example is: When I need money, I will promise repayment while intending not to repay in order to obtain a loan. Other defensible examples are acceptable.

Universal law test for the failing maxim: If everyone in these circumstances made insincere promises, lenders would not trust those assurances. The promise could no longer secure the loan through the lender's belief in it, so the universalized maxim undermines the means its purpose requires. This is a contradiction in conception. Common slip: rejecting the maxim only because lenders would lose money, rather than explaining its self-defeat.

Your partner's verdict: Answers depend on the maxims exchanged. A satisfactory sentence identifies agreement or disagreement, names the relevant feature of the test, and gives a reason. For example: I agree that your false-promise maxim fails because universalizing it removes the trust needed to obtain the loan. If students disagree, look for a specific challenge to the maxim's description, the alleged contradiction, or its rational willability. Common slip: treating personal approval or dislike as the universal law test.

Problems

items: In Groundwork section II, Kant gives four examples. One is a prosperous person who decides to give nothing to others in need. Can this maxim be universalized without contradiction? Kant says it still fails. How does its failure differ from that of the false promise?

Suppose, in a hypothetical case, a recruiter tells applicants a position is paid when it is unpaid, to get free work. Another recruiter honestly offers a low-paid job that applicants may refuse. On the humanity formula, which treats the applicants merely as means, and what does consent have to do with it?

Suppose one person's maxim is 'I will lie whenever it suits me' and another's is 'I will lie to a murderer to save an innocent life'. The first fails the universal law test. Does the second? Does the result show that the test depends on how the maxim is described?

Mill and Kant both say lying is normally wrong. Suppose, in a hypothetical case, a lie would save a friend from a murderer. Is their disagreement about the facts of what a lie would cause, or about something else?

handouts.key:
1. A universal practice of refusing assistance is conceivable: people could pursue their purposes without helping others. It therefore avoids the contradiction in conception found in false promising. Kant argues that a rational agent cannot will this practice universally because the agent may need others' help in pursuing ends. It involves a contradiction in will and grounds an imperfect duty of beneficence. False promising instead undermines the trust on which its own success depends. Look for the distinction between conceiving a universal practice and rationally willing it. Common slip: saying that every conceivable maxim passes. See Kant, Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals, section II.

2. The deceptive recruiter treats applicants merely as means. Applicants agree on the false understanding that the work is paid; they cannot make an informed choice about the actual arrangement. The honest recruiter allows an informed decision about the stated terms. However, an opportunity to refuse does not by itself establish that the arrangement fully respects persons: coercion, exploitation, and other conditions may still matter. Look for an explanation connecting deception to the bypassing of rational agency. Common slip: treating any use of another person's labor as mere use, or treating consent as sufficient to settle every moral concern. See Kant, Groundwork, section II.

3. The protective maxim needs its own universalization argument. Students should ask whether a universal practice of lying to murderers would frustrate the lie's protective purpose and whether a rational agent could will that practice. If murderers reliably expected false answers, deception might cease to protect the intended victim; students must explain the circumstances rather than assume this outcome. The continued existence of ordinary trust does not alone establish that this narrower maxim passes. The comparison shows why the description of a maxim matters, but does not prove that any preferred verdict can legitimately be obtained. Look for a maxim that expresses the agent's actual circumstances, action, and purpose without arbitrary exceptions. Common slip: assuming that a good purpose automatically makes a maxim universalizable. Distinguish this interpretive argument from Kant's rejection of lying in On a Supposed Right to Lie from Philanthropy.

4. Their disagreement can persist even when both accept that the lie saves the friend. Kant rejects lying as a violation of duty; its permissibility does not turn on a calculation of beneficial consequences. Mill treats truthfulness as a highly important moral rule but recognizes exceptions, including withholding information from a wrongdoer when needed to prevent grave harm and when withholding requires denial. In the stipulated case, the lie is justified by the protection it provides, with due attention to the wider importance of trust. Look for the difference between an exceptionless duty and a rule justified by utility. Common slip: reducing Mill's view to whatever immediately benefits the speaker. Silence or refusal is relevant only if it actually protects the friend in the case being discussed. See Kant's essay and Mill, Utilitarianism, chapter 2.

segments.title: Aristotle’s question: how to live well
segments.description:
The teacher sets out Aristotle’s starting point: ethics asks what makes a human life go well. His answer is eudaimonia, flourishing, which is an activity of the soul in accordance with virtue over a whole life.
The teacher distinguishes virtues of intellect from virtues of character, which are the topic of book II. Then each student writes yes or no, with one reason, to the question on the screen, and a partner compares.
The teacher hears two answers and uses them to show why flourishing needs a settled character.
segments.teacherNotes: Book I is background, so give it in your own words. Aristotle’s point is that a single swallow does not make a spring: one good day does not make a good life. Expect ‘no, it is a whole life’. Link to the traits students listed.
shown: Can a person flourish in a single afternoon? Write yes or no and one reason.

segments.title: How virtues are acquired: habituation
segments.description:
The teacher presents Aristotle’s claim from book II, chapters 1 to 4: virtues of character come neither from nature nor against it. We are capable of them and complete them by habit, as builders become builders by building.
The teacher poses the puzzle on the screen. Each student writes a one-sentence answer for how Aristotle might reply, and a partner compares.
The teacher then gives Aristotle’s reply: learners act under guidance, as people learn grammar or music, until they act knowingly, for the act’s own sake, from a firm character. The teacher adds that enjoying the right act is the sign of a formed virtue.
segments.teacherNotes: Misconception: habituation means mindless routine. Aristotle requires knowing, choosing the act for itself and acting from a firm state (book II, chapter 4). Link to the lawmaker who makes citizens good by habituating them. Rachels, chapter 12, makes the same point in his own words.
shown: If we become just by doing just acts, how can anyone do a just act before they are just?
Steps: guided practice → the act becomes easier → we come to enjoy it → settled character

segments.title: Break
segments.description: Students take a short break. The puzzle about doing just acts stays on the screen.
shown: If we become just by doing just acts, how can anyone do a just act before they are just?

segments.title: The doctrine of the mean
segments.description:
The teacher explains that too much or too little destroys, as with food and exercise, and that a virtue is a state that hits the mean in feeling and action. Each student first writes the excess, the deficiency and the mean for anger, and a partner checks.
The teacher then shows Aristotle’s pairs, with courage as the worked case: fear and confidence, with cowardice, courage and rashness. The teacher uses Aristotle’s trainer example: if ten pounds of food is too much and two too little for a particular person, the trainer will not simply order six.
The teacher says the mean is relative to us and set by practical wisdom.
segments.teacherNotes: Anger: excess is short temper, deficiency inirascibility, mean mildness. The mean is not the numerical middle. Aristotle (book II, chapter 6) says it concerns the right time, object, person, aim and manner. The wrestler Milo needs more food than a beginner.

segments.title: Find the mistake in a draft
segments.description:
A draft paragraph on the screen misreads the doctrine of the mean. Each student writes the main mistake and a corrected sentence in four minutes.
Partners compare for two minutes. The teacher hears two corrections and states the right reading, using courage.
segments.teacherNotes: Mistake: treating the mean as an arithmetic average that is the same for everyone. Correction: the mean is relative to the person and situation, fixed by practical wisdom, and for a trained soldier and a novice the courageous act differs. Also acceptable: some acts, such as murder, have no mean (book II, chapter 6).
shown: Draft: Aristotle says virtue is a mean, so the virtuous person is moderate in everything. A soldier who feels a middling amount of fear, neither the most nor the least, is courageous. Courage is therefore the average of cowardice and rashness, and the same amount of fear is right for everyone.

segments.title: What kind of person versus which act
segments.description:
The case on the screen has two versions. Each student writes one sentence per theory on whether Mill, Kant and Aristotle would see a difference between version A and version B, and a partner compares.
The teacher hears two and then sets the three guiding questions side by side. The teacher closes with the main objection: advice such as ‘do what the virtuous person would do’ may not guide action in a dilemma, and may be circular.
segments.teacherNotes: Mill: motive does not change an act’s rightness, as seen earlier in the course. Kant: only acting from duty has moral worth, so he too cares about motive. Aristotle adds settled character and fitting feeling, not duty alone. Rachels, chapter 12, discusses the guidance objection; leave it for the seminar.

Side by side: Utilitarianism: which act produces the most happiness for everyone affected? | Kant: can the maxim be willed as a universal law, and does the act treat persons as ends? | Aristotle: what would a person of good character do, and what kind of person am I becoming?

segments.title: Close of the lecture
segments.description:
The teacher states the takeaway: Aristotle asks what kind of person to be, holds that virtues are acquired by habit, and defines each as a mean between excess and deficiency relative to us.
Students are told that next time is the seminar. They bring Aristotle, book II, Rachels, chapter 12, and the discussion questions they prepared from them. Copies of the participation brief will be handed out again.
A short practice quiz on this meeting is available after class and counts toward no grade.

segments.title: How this seminar runs
segments.description:
The teacher hands out copies of the Seminar participation brief and rubric, with this meeting’s problems printed with them. In two minutes the teacher states that Seminar participation counts for 10% of the course grade and is scored on Preparation and on Contribution and listening.
The teacher explains the format: students lead, the teacher listens and scores as it happens, and gives a synthesis at the end. Students sit in their groups of four.
segments.teacherNotes: Keep exposition short. Nothing is collected. Scores are recorded as the discussion runs, on the rubric’s levels. The next group on the rota leads. The group that led at the previous seminar is scored on listening.

segments.title: Choose your questions
segments.description:
Each student reads the four problems printed with the brief. Each student rereads the discussion questions they prepared from Aristotle, book II, and Rachels, chapter 12, and chooses the one they think will best advance discussion of the reading.
The teacher walks round and notes who has questions written.
segments.teacherNotes:
Questions are the student’s own; do not supply or correct them. Students use their own copies. Problems printed with the brief, and answers:
1. Aristotle says the mean is relative to us, not the arithmetic middle (book II, chapter 6, the trainer and the wrestler Milo). Is this a strength or a weakness of the doctrine? Answer: strength, since right action depends on person and situation; weakness, since it gives no rule for finding the mean, only the judgment of the practically wise.
2. We become just by doing just acts (book II, chapter 1). Yet a just act seems to need a just person. How does Aristotle answer in chapter 4, and is the answer enough? Answer: the learner acts under guidance; a virtuous act also needs knowledge, choice for its own sake and a firm character. Critics ask what moves the learner at first.
3. Suppose one person returns a lost wallet from honesty and another only from fear of a camera. Act-based theories may give the same verdict on the act. What does virtue ethics add, and is it right to add it? Answer: virtue ethics emphasizes settled character and fitting feeling, which help explain what each person would do when unobserved. Kant also distinguishes motives: acting from duty gives an act moral worth. Returning the wallet from honesty does not by itself establish that the person acts from duty. The comparison concerns character as well as the rightness of the act.
4. Aristotle says some acts, such as murder, have no mean (book II, chapter 6). Why, and does that limit the doctrine? Answer: some names already include wrongness, so there is no right amount of them. It shows that the mean does not apply to every action: some actions are already wrongful, rather than admitting a right response between excess and deficiency.

segments.title: Group discussion led by students
segments.description:
The next group on the rota sits in the middle and leads. Each member in turn has three and a half minutes to present their chosen question, invite responses, keep the talk on reasons and state where the group stands. Allow the remaining two minutes for transitions between presenters.
The teacher listens to this group only and scores its four students on leading as it happens. Other groups listen, and each student notes one claim to take up and one challenge to bring.
The group that led at the previous seminar is among the listeners, and the teacher scores its four students on listening in the next two segments.
segments.teacherNotes: Judge contribution by the quality of reasons and by listening, not volume. Each group is observed leading one week and listening the next. Do not rescue a stalled question. Intervene only to hold time between presenters.

segments.title: Agree the sharpest disagreement
segments.description:
In their groups, each student states in a sentence the claim they would take up and the challenge they would bring. Each group, the leading group too, then agrees one sentence stating the sharpest disagreement they heard and writes it down for the report.
The teacher listens to the group that led at the previous seminar and scores its four students on listening.
segments.teacherNotes: Push for a sentence naming the claim or premise at issue, not a topic. Example: whether a mean that depends on the person can still guide anyone. Use each student’s claim, challenge and engagement as evidence for the rubric.

segments.title: Whole-class discussion and synthesis
segments.description:
One student from each group reports its sharpest disagreement in one sentence. Everyone writes a one-line answer to this question: is it a defect in an ethical theory if it cannot say what to do in a dilemma, or is it enough that it tells us what kind of person to be? Why?
Three answers are heard. The teacher closes with a board summary of habituation, the mean, and the contrast between asking what to do and asking what to be.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected: a defect if the theory claims to settle right and wrong; less so if its aim is flourishing. Press students to say what a person of practical wisdom does when two virtues conflict, such as honesty and kindness. Board: habituation; the mean (courage); act versus character; guidance objection.

segments.title: Close and what comes next
segments.description:
The teacher states the takeaway: for Aristotle, virtue is a habit of choosing the mean, built by practice, and the strongest objection is whether it can guide action.
The teacher sets the Weekly reading responses (20%) on Hobbes and Rachels, due at the first meeting of Social contract theory. The teacher reminds students that the Paper defending one theory (20%) is also due at that meeting.
The lecture in Social contract theory examines Hobbes’s state of nature and the case for a sovereign. Students read Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, chapters 13 to 15, and James Rachels and Stuart Rachels, The Elements of Moral Philosophy, chapter 6, and prepare discussion questions.

keyIdeas: Aristotle starts from a different question than Mill and Kant. He asks how a person should live to flourish (eudaimonia) and what kind of person to become, not first which act is right.

Virtues of character are acquired by habituation. We become just by doing just acts, builders by building, and with guidance the doing becomes a settled state in which the right act is chosen for its own sake and enjoyed.
A virtue is a settled state of choosing and feeling well, which lies in a mean between an excess and a deficiency. Courage lies between cowardice and rashness.
The mean is not an arithmetic average. It is relative to us, set by the judgment of a person of practical wisdom, and some acts, such as murder, have no mean at all.
Virtue ethics gives different weight to motive, feeling and long-term character than act-based theories do. Its main challenge is whether it can tell us what to do in a dilemma.

vocabulary.definition: Aristotle’s word for flourishing, a complete human life lived in accordance with virtue.
A settled state of character that disposes us to choose and feel as we should.
A settled state of character that disposes us to feel and choose wrongly, through excess or deficiency.
Becoming virtuous by repeatedly doing virtuous acts under guidance until they become second nature.
Aristotle’s claim that a virtue lies between two vices, one of excess and one of deficiency.
Too much of a feeling or action, such as the excessive confidence of rashness in the face of danger.
Too little of a feeling or action, such as the deficient confidence of cowardice in the face of danger.
The judgment of the person who sees what a situation calls for, by which the mean is fixed.
