study.overview: Aristotle’s Nicomachean Ethics, book II, starts from a different question than Mill or Kant. He does not ask first which act is right. He asks how a person should live to flourish (eudaimonia) and what kind of person to become. For him flourishing is an activity of the soul in accordance with virtue over a whole life, not one good afternoon. This guide covers three ideas from book II: how character virtues are acquired by habit, how each virtue is a mean between two extremes, and how asking what kind of person to be differs from asking which act to do. It ends with the main objection to this approach. Read it alongside Rachels, chapter 12.

points.heading: Virtues are acquired by habituation
points.explanation: Aristotle holds that virtues of character come neither from nature nor against it (book II, chapters 1 to 4 (to confirm)). We are able to acquire them, and we complete them through practice, as people become builders by building. We become just by doing just acts and brave by doing brave acts. This does not mean mindless routine. A learner first acts under guidance, as when learning grammar or music. In time the person acts knowingly, chooses the act for its own sake and acts from a firm, settled state. Enjoying the right act is a sign that the virtue has formed. Example: a trainee nurse is coached to stay patient with anxious patients. At first it takes effort and she follows her supervisor’s example. After years of practice she is patient without strain, knows why it matters, and takes satisfaction in it. The repeated acts have become her character.

points.heading: The doctrine of the mean
points.explanation: A virtue is a settled state of choosing and feeling well. It lies in a mean between an excess and a deficiency, because too much or too little of a feeling or action spoils it, as too much or too little food and exercise spoils health. Courage, which concerns fear and confidence, lies between cowardice (deficiency) and rashness (excess). Suppose an engineer sees a safety fault and must decide whether to report it. The coward stays silent out of fear. The rash person makes a public scene before checking the facts. The courageous person raises it with the right people, at the right time, in the right way. Anger works the same way: short temper is the excess, inirascibility (almost never getting angry) is the deficiency, and mildness is the mean. The mean is not an arithmetic average and is not the same for everyone. Aristotle’s trainer example (book II, chapter 6) makes the point. If ten pounds of food is too much and two too little for a particular person, the trainer will not simply prescribe six, because the wrestler Milo needs far more than a beginner. The mean depends on the right time, object, person, aim and manner, and it is fixed by the judgment of a person of practical wisdom.

points.heading: What kind of person versus which act
points.explanation: Act-based theories begin with the act. Utilitarianism asks which act produces the most happiness for everyone affected. Kant asks whether the maxim can be willed as a universal law and whether the act treats persons as ends. Aristotle asks what a person of good character would do and what kind of person I am becoming. This shifts the weight toward motive, feeling and long-term character. Example: Dev volunteers at a shelter every week because he cares about the people there. Sam goes every week only because a scholarship requires the hours. The two acts and their effects on the shelter are the same. For Mill, motive does not change an act’s rightness. Kant does care about motive, since only acting from duty has moral worth. Aristotle adds something further: a settled character and fitting feeling, so that the right act is chosen for its own sake and enjoyed. Ask what each theory would say about Dev and Sam, and where their answers part.

points.heading: The main objection: can it guide action?
points.explanation: The strongest challenge to virtue ethics is practical. Advice such as ‘do what the virtuous person would do’ may not help in a dilemma, and it may be circular, since we seem to need to know what is right in order to identify the virtuous person. Consider a case where honesty and kindness pull apart, such as deciding how much of a harsh truth to tell a friend who is grieving. Aristotle’s answer points to practical wisdom, but critics say this names the skill without saying how to exercise it. Rachels discusses this objection in chapter 12. To test it, take a dilemma of your own and ask what a practically wise person would do and how you could tell. Then decide whether a theory must settle such cases to count as a good account of morality, or whether telling us what kind of person to be is enough.

handouts.title: Seminar participation: problems for this meeting
handouts.copies: One per student, printed with the Seminar participation brief and rubric

blocks.text: Read the four problems below. Then reread the discussion questions you prepared from Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, book II, and Rachels, The Elements of Moral Philosophy, chapter 12. Choose the question you think will best advance discussion of the reading.
Problems

items: Aristotle says the mean is relative to us, not the arithmetic middle (book II, chapter 6, the trainer and the wrestler Milo). Is this a strength or a weakness of the doctrine?
We become just by doing just acts (book II, chapter 1). Yet a just act seems to need a just person. How does Aristotle answer in chapter 4 (to confirm), and is the answer enough?

Suppose one person returns a lost wallet from honesty and another only from fear of a camera. Act-based theories may give the same verdict on the act. What does virtue ethics add, and is it right to add it?
Aristotle says some acts, such as murder, have no mean (book II, chapter 6). Why, and does that limit the doctrine?

blocks.hint: The question I choose, in my own words (one of the four above or one I prepared)

handouts.key:
1. The mean relative to us: A strength is sensitivity to relevant differences in ability, circumstances, danger and responsibility. Courage requires an appropriate response to fear and confidence, rather than the same behavior from everyone. A weakness is that this leaves difficult judgments about what is appropriate. Aristotle supplies a rational standard—the judgment of a practically wise person—rather than an arithmetic procedure (Nicomachean Ethics, II.6). Look for a reasoned assessment of whether this offers adequate guidance. Common slip: treating “relative to us” as meaning that whatever someone prefers is virtuous.

2. Acquiring justice: Distinguish doing an action of the kind a just person would do from doing it as a just person does. A learner can perform appropriate actions through instruction and practice before possessing a settled virtue. Acting virtuously additionally requires knowledge, choosing the action for its own sake, and acting from a firm character (II.1, II.4). A strong evaluation explains how practice can develop character, or questions whether repetition and guidance adequately explain the development of virtuous motivation. Common slip: assuming that outwardly correct behavior already proves that someone is virtuous.

3. Returning the wallet: Both people perform the same outward action, but their motives and dispositions differ. Returning it from honesty can express a stable commitment to honest conduct; returning it only because of a camera does not establish that commitment. Virtue ethics also considers appropriate feelings and whether honest conduct is dependable across circumstances. The example alone does not establish either person's whole character. Students may defend attention to character because it explains moral reliability, or argue that assessing an action's rightness remains a separate task. Mill distinguishes an action's rightness from the agent's motive and character (Utilitarianism, chapter 2). Kant distinguishes acting in accordance with duty from acting from duty; honesty alone does not establish action from duty (Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals, section I). Common slip: claiming that all act-based theories ignore motives or that Kant gives the two agents identical assessments of moral worth.

4. Acts with no mean: Aristotle treats terms such as murder as already identifying wrongful action. There is no appropriate person, occasion or manner in which to commit murder virtuously. The doctrine therefore does not prescribe moderation in everything: some actions are excluded rather than balanced between excess and deficiency (II.6). Students may see this as a sensible boundary or ask whether the doctrine needs a further account of why these actions are wrong. Common slip: proposing a moderate amount of murder as the virtuous mean.

The question I choose, in my own words: Answers vary. Look for a clearly formulated question grounded in the assigned reading that opens a substantive issue about habituation, the mean, character or action guidance. Students may choose a printed problem or a question they prepared. A strong answer identifies something that reasons and textual interpretation could help resolve. Common slip: supplying only a topic, such as “courage,” instead of a question.

l_69f8e85702a7.summary: Examines Hobbes's state of nature and the case for a sovereign; the paper defending one theory is handed in at the start.
readings: Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, ch. 13 to 15 (to confirm)
James Rachels and Stuart Rachels, The Elements of Moral Philosophy, ch. 6 (to confirm)

segments.title: Papers and responses due now; life with no enforcement
segments.description:
The teacher says that the Paper defending one theory (20%) is due now, and so are the Weekly reading responses (20%) on Hobbes and Rachels, chapter 6. Each is a student’s own work.
Each student writes yes or no, with one reason, to the question on the screen. Partners compare for two minutes, and the teacher hears two or three answers.
The teacher says that today’s reading asks what would happen if the answer were no for everyone.
segments.teacherNotes: Expect most to say yes at first, then hedge about strangers. Mark the reasons that rest on trust in others, since Hobbes builds on that. Do not ask anyone to confess something they have done.
shown: Suppose that for one week there were no police, no courts and no enforcement of any rule in your city. Would you keep to the rules you follow now? Say yes or no, and give one reason.

segments.title: Hobbes’s state of nature and its three causes of quarrel
segments.description:
The teacher presents Leviathan, chapter 13. Hobbes starts from rough equality: the weakest can kill the strongest by cunning or by allying with others.
The teacher names the three causes of quarrel: competition, diffidence and glory. The state of nature is life with no common power, so each has a right to everything and no one is safe.
After examining the table, each student predicts which causes would remain if goods were plentiful for everyone. A partner compares, and the teacher hears two.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected: diffidence and glory remain, which is why plenty does not end the war. Hobbes writes the state of nature as a thought experiment about life without government; he does not claim people are wicked. Chapter 13 gives the description, so paraphrase it.
shown: Table: Cause of quarrel | What drives it / Competition | Gain: people want the same scarce goods / Diffidence | Safety: fear that others will strike first / Glory | Reputation: the wish to be respected

segments.title: Which cause of quarrel is at work?
segments.description:
Each student reads the three hypothetical cases on the screen and labels each with the cause of quarrel that best explains it. Partners compare labels and settle any difference by pointing to the cause in the case.
The teacher hears one disagreement and resolves it.
segments.teacherNotes:
Cases and answers:
1. Two farmers need the one spring in a dry year. Competition.
2. A farmer who fears his neighbor will attack strikes first, though he wants nothing from him. Diffidence.
3. A chief raids a village that mocked him, taking nothing. Glory.
Case 2 is the usual confusion: it is defensive, not greedy.
shown: Case 1: Two farmers depend on the same spring. In a dry year there is water for only one farm.
Case 2: A farmer has heard that his neighbor is arming. He has no wish for his neighbor’s land, but he attacks first to be safe.
Case 3: A village mocks a local chief. He leads a raid on it and takes nothing, because he wants to be feared.

segments.title: From self-preservation to the laws of nature
segments.description:
The teacher presents chapters 14 and 15. Everyone wants to survive, and reason finds precepts that serve survival. These are the laws of nature.
The teacher gives the first law, to seek peace where it can be had, and the second, to give up the right to everything if others will do the same. The third is to keep the covenants made, and justice is keeping them.
Students then write in one sentence why the second law is rational and not merely generous, and a partner checks.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected: giving up the right to everything is safer than a war where anyone can kill you. Hobbes says reason discovers the laws of nature through reflection on self-preservation. Say this in your own words. Rachels, chapter 6, gives the same route to morality.
shown: Steps: Want to survive → Peace is the best route → Give up the right to everything if others will → Keep the covenants made

segments.title: Work the prisoner’s dilemma
segments.description:
The table on the screen shows a hypothetical choice between two neighboring villages. Each student predicts what each village will do and why, and writes it down. Partners compare.
The teacher then asks which outcome benefits both villages more, and why each has an incentive to arm under the stated payoffs.
The teacher links this to Rachels, chapter 6, and to the need for enforcement.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected: whatever B does, A scores higher by arming (4 against 3, 1 against 0). B reasons the same, so both arm and each scores 1, not 3. Both disarming is better for each, but neither can trust the other. The numbers are hypothetical.
shown: Two neighboring villages each choose to disarm or to arm. Scores show how safe each village ends up, out of 4.
Table: | Village B disarms | Village B arms / Village A disarms | A 3, B 3 | A 0, B 4 / Village A arms | A 4, B 0 | A 1, B 1

segments.title: Break
segments.description: Students take a short break. The table of scores stays on the screen.

segments.title: The case for a sovereign and the Foole
segments.description:
The teacher explains why Hobbes concludes that covenants need a power to enforce them: keeping faith without assurance that others will do so can endanger self-preservation. People therefore authorize a sovereign. This is developed in Leviathan, chapters 17 and 18, after the assigned reading.
The teacher then sets out the Foole’s challenge in chapter 15: it can be reasonable to break a covenant when it pays. Hobbes replies that a person who breaks covenants cannot expect others to admit him to cooperation.
Each student writes one sentence on whether the Foole’s reasoning works for a person who is never caught. A partner compares.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected: students split. Ask whether Hobbes’s appeal to exclusion answers the case of an undetected breach. In chapter 15, he also argues that an unexpectedly successful breach does not establish that choosing it was reasonable. Chapters 17 and 18 are beyond the assigned reading, so give them in your own words and do not quote.
shown: Steps: No enforcement → Each fears keeping faith alone → Covenants fail → A sovereign with power to punish → Covenants hold

segments.title: Choose between two readings of Hobbes
segments.description:
The screen shows two readings of where morality comes from for Hobbes. Each student chooses the more accurate reading and writes two sentences of reasons. Partners compare, then the teacher hears two answers.
The teacher states which reading fits chapters 14 and 15 better and what is true in the other.
segments.teacherNotes: Reading B fits better: the laws of nature are found by reason from self-preservation, and the sovereign makes obedience safe. Reading A is true of civil law, whose content the sovereign fixes. Common mistake: treating Hobbes as a mere power theorist.
shown: Reading A: For Hobbes, morality is whatever the sovereign commands. Without a sovereign there is no right or wrong at all.
Reading B: For Hobbes, reason shows what each must do to survive, and those rules hold in principle before any sovereign. The sovereign makes it safe to follow them.

segments.title: Is morality a convenient agreement?
segments.description:
The teacher puts the claim on the screen. Each student writes one reason for it and one reason against it, using Hobbes and Rachels, chapter 6. Partners compare.
The teacher hears two reasons on each side and lists them on the board. The teacher says the seminar will test these reasons.
segments.teacherNotes: For: it explains why morality benefits everyone and why we need enforcement. Against: it struggles to explain duties to infants and animals who cannot bargain, and to distant strangers outside the agreement, and it seems to make cruelty wrong only when it is risky. Do not settle it.
shown: Claim: Morality is a convenient agreement among self-interested people, made because each does better with the rules than without them.

segments.title: Close of the lecture
segments.description:
The teacher states the takeaway: Hobbes derives peace-seeking rules from self-preservation, and the dilemma of trust leads him to a sovereign.
Students are told that next time is the seminar. They bring Hobbes, chapters 13 to 15, Rachels, chapter 6, and the discussion questions they prepared from them. Copies of the participation brief will be handed out again.
A short practice quiz on this meeting is available after class and counts toward no grade.
segments.teacherNotes: Remind students that preparation is part of the seminar score. Nothing is collected.

segments.title: How this seminar runs
segments.description:
The teacher hands out copies of the Seminar participation brief and rubric, with this meeting’s problems printed with them.
The teacher states that Seminar participation counts for 10% of the course grade and is scored on Preparation and on Contribution and listening. Students lead, the teacher listens and scores as it happens, and gives a synthesis at the end.
Students sit in their groups of four.
segments.teacherNotes: Keep exposition short. Nothing is collected. Scores are recorded as the discussion runs, on the rubric’s levels. The group that led at the previous seminar is scored on listening today.

segments.title: Choose your questions
segments.description:
Each student reads the four problems printed with the brief. Each student rereads the discussion questions they prepared from Hobbes, chapters 13 to 15, and Rachels, chapter 6.
Each chooses the question they think will best advance discussion of the reading. The teacher walks round and notes who has questions written.
segments.teacherNotes:
Questions are the student’s own; do not supply or correct them. Students use their own copies.
Problems printed with the brief, and answers:
1. Hobbes names competition, diffidence and glory as causes of quarrel (chapter 13). Is diffidence alone enough to cause war among moderate people? Answer: diffidence can generate conflict even among moderate people when they lack reliable assurances and reasonably see preemptive attack as their safest option. A mere possibility of attack does not establish that everyone should strike first.
2. Hobbes derives the law to keep covenants from self-preservation (chapters 14 and 15). Does the Foole show that breaking a covenant can be rational? Answer: Hobbes argues that a known covenant-breaker risks exclusion from cooperation and that accidental success does not make a breach a reasonable choice. Whether this answers a reliably undetected breach remains open to challenge.
3. Rachels, chapter 6, asks whom the social contract theory leaves out. Can a theory built on mutual advantage explain duties to infants, animals or distant strangers? Answer: infants and animals cannot bargain directly; distant strangers may be able to bargain but remain outside the agreement. Contractors’ concern for others can support some protections, but students should ask whether it grounds duties to everyone affected.
4. Suppose Hobbes is right that any sovereign is better than the state of nature. Does it follow that we must obey a cruel one? Answer: Hobbes generally requires obedience even to a harsh sovereign, but subjects retain the liberty to defend their own lives, and their obligation depends on protection. Critics can also challenge the premise that unchecked rule is always preferable.

segments.title: Group discussion led by students
segments.description:
The next group on the rota sits in the middle and leads. Each member in turn has three and a half minutes to present their chosen question, invite responses, keep the talk on reasons and state where the group stands.
Two minutes remain for transitions between presenters.
The teacher listens to this group only and scores its four students on leading as it happens. Other groups listen, and each student notes one claim to take up and one challenge to bring.
segments.teacherNotes: Judge contribution by the quality of reasons and by listening, not volume. Each group is observed leading one week and listening the next. Do not rescue a stalled question. Intervene only to hold time between presenters. The group that led at the previous seminar is among the listeners.

segments.title: Agree the sharpest disagreement
segments.description:
In their groups, each student states in a sentence the claim they would take up and the challenge they would bring.
Each group, the leading group too, then agrees one sentence stating the sharpest disagreement they heard and writes it down for the report.
The teacher listens to the group that led at the previous seminar and scores its four students on listening.
segments.teacherNotes: Push for a sentence naming the claim or premise at issue, not a topic. Example: whether fear of being cheated is enough to make breaking a covenant rational. Use each student’s claim, challenge and engagement as evidence for the rubric.

segments.title: Whole-class discussion and synthesis
segments.description:
One student from each group reports its sharpest disagreement in one sentence.
Everyone writes a one-line answer to this question: if morality is an agreement among self-interested people, does that explain what morality is, or does it explain it away? Why? Three answers are heard.
The teacher closes with a board summary of the state of nature, the laws of nature and the sovereign, then the objection from those who cannot bargain.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected: it explains why we have rules but not why they bind us to those with no power. Press students to say whether Hobbes’s justification is moral or prudential. Board: three causes of quarrel; laws of nature; dilemma and sovereign; who is left out.

segments.title: Close and what comes next
segments.description:
The teacher states the takeaway: for Hobbes, rules of peace follow from self-preservation, and the best objection asks who is left out of an agreement made for mutual advantage.
The teacher sets the Weekly reading responses (20%) on Judith Jarvis Thomson, “The Trolley Problem”, due at the first meeting of The theories tested on hard cases.
The lecture in The theories tested on hard cases applies utilitarian, Kantian, virtue and contract theories to Thomson’s trolley, footbridge and transplant cases and compares their verdicts. Students read Thomson, “The Trolley Problem”, before then and prepare discussion questions.
segments.teacherNotes: Remind students that the response is each student’s own work. Tell them to bring their copy of Thomson.

keyIdeas: Hobbes’s state of nature is what life would be like with no common power over people. Because people are roughly equal in strength and cunning, each can threaten any other. Three causes of quarrel produce a state of war: competition for gain, diffidence (fear for one’s safety) and glory (concern for reputation).

Hobbes derives the laws of nature from self-preservation. Reason tells each person to seek peace, to give up the right to all things if others will too, and to keep the covenants made. Justice, for Hobbes, is keeping covenants.

The prisoner’s dilemma shows why reason alone does not secure peace. Each side does better by breaking the agreement whatever the other does, so both end up worse off. This is Hobbes’s case for a sovereign with the power to enforce covenants.

If Hobbes is right, morality looks like a convenient agreement among self-interested people. The Foole’s challenge and the problem of duties to those unable to bargain, such as infants and animals, and to distant strangers outside an agreement test this claim.

vocabulary.definition: Hobbes’s thought experiment of human life with no common power to keep order, in which each person judges for themselves and no one is safe.
In Hobbes, distrust or fear of others, which leads people to strike first for their own safety.
For Hobbes, each person’s liberty to use their own power to preserve their life, which in the state of nature extends to everything.
A rule found by reason that forbids what destroys one’s life and tells one to do what preserves it, such as seeking peace.
An agreement in which one party promises to perform later; for Hobbes, keeping covenants is the content of justice.
A situation in which each party does better by breaking an agreement whatever the other does, yet both are worse off if both break it.
In Hobbes, the person or body authorized to hold the power that enforces covenants and keeps the peace.
The view that morality or political authority rests on an agreement that rational people would make for mutual benefit.

t_ca7364fb446c.prompt: Does impartial concern for interests settle what should have been done for Baby Theresa? Why or why not?
followUps: Look at the interests you marked in your two columns. If every affected individual’s interests count equally, does that tell us which interests should win?
Suppose one of your reasons appeals only to what her parents wanted. Is that a reason that could persuade someone who is not her parent, and what does the minimum conception say about it?
What would you need to add to reasons and equal weight to reach a verdict, and where in Rachels and Rachels, chapter 1, do you see the authors doing that?

t_bcecf5e5218e.prompt: Does an infant who will never be conscious have interests?
followUps: Is an interest in avoiding suffering the only kind of interest there is, or can someone have an interest in continued life or in bodily integrity without feeling anything?

If you decide that Baby Theresa had no interests of her own, does it follow that only the interests of the infants waiting for transplants and of her parents count? What else would you have to defend?
Would your answer change for a newborn who will become conscious, or for an adult in a permanent coma? What does the difference between them show about what you take an interest to be?

t_d8c7e3e7395f.prompt: Suppose Lena argues that a town should protect a public park only because her friends use it. Which response best applies the minimum conception of morality?

choices.text: Give priority to Lena’s friends because she knows their interests best.
Accept Lena’s view if she feels strongly enough about the park.
Count only the interests of people who use the park most often.
Consider the interests of everyone affected, including people outside Lena’s circle.

t_d8c7e3e7395f.explanation: The minimum conception calls for reasons and impartial concern for affected individuals’ interests. “Give priority to Lena’s friends” favors people because of their connection to her. “Accept Lena’s view” treats feeling alone as justification. “Count only the interests of people who use the park most often” excludes others whose interests may be affected.

t_3578ada85e20.prompt: Suppose a student changes her judgment about a school policy after hearing a stronger reason against it. This revision can be consistent with the minimum conception of morality.

choices.text: True
False

t_3578ada85e20.explanation: Guiding conduct by reason includes being open to revising a judgment when better reasons emerge. Revision alone does not show whether the student has also considered everyone’s interests impartially.

t_42e2344b5994.prompt: Suppose a hospital has one available treatment and two patients who could benefit. A student says, “The minimum conception tells us to give it to the patient who gains the most, so the case is settled.” Identify the mistake and rewrite the claim so it is accurate.
t_42e2344b5994.answer: The student mistakes the minimum conception for a rule that requires maximizing benefits. The conception requires us to give reasons and consider both patients’ interests impartially, but further argument is needed to decide how to weigh those interests and allocate the treatment.
t_42e2344b5994.explanation: Reason and impartiality constrain the decision, but they do not by themselves prescribe a maximizing rule or settle how competing interests should be weighed.

t_8785e54483fa.prompt: Suppose a town must decide whether to close a bridge for repairs, making some residents’ journeys longer while reducing a safety risk. Which question best applies impartial concern to the case?

choices.text: Which residents have the closest ties to the town’s officials?
Which decision produces the strongest feeling among bridge users?
What interests of residents and other affected people are at stake?
What decision would treat every resident in exactly the same way?

t_8785e54483fa.explanation: The correct question identifies whose interests need consideration. “Which residents have the closest ties” invites favoritism. “Which decision produces the strongest feeling” treats feeling as sufficient justification. “What decision would treat every resident in exactly the same way” confuses equal consideration with identical treatment.

t_ddd16b48715f.prompt: Suppose an assigned reading argues that a city should restrict private cars because traffic harms public health. Which question would best open a seminar discussion of the reading’s reasoning?

choices.text: Does the health argument justify restricting cars?
How many paragraphs discuss the health argument?
When was the reading on traffic published?
How often does the author mention public health?

t_ddd16b48715f.explanation: The correct question invites discussion of whether the author’s reason supports the claim. “How many paragraphs” concerns the text’s structure rather than its reasoning. “When was the reading” asks for a publication fact. “How often does the author” asks about wording without examining the argument.

t_9fab4584b9dd.title: Seminar participation
t_9fab4584b9dd.prompt: Seminar participation counts for 10% of the course grade. Attendance at seminars is expected. Read the assigned texts before the seminar, bring them with you, and prepare discussion questions in advance. Participation is assessed individually on preparation and contribution, using the rubric below. How often you speak does not determine your score.
steps: Review the discussion questions you prepared from the assigned reading alongside the questions or problems handed out or shown at the meeting. Choose the question you think will best advance discussion of the reading.
When your group leads, present your chosen question, invite others to respond, keep the discussion focused on reasons, and state where the group stands.

When another group leads, listen to its discussion. Note a claim you would take up and a challenge you would bring to a claim or reason. With your group, agree on a sentence stating the sharpest disagreement you heard.
Take part in the whole-class discussion of the questions or problems handed out or shown at the meeting. Consider the reasons offered by others as you develop your contribution.
t_9fab4584b9dd.answerKey:
1. Assess each student’s prepared questions for engagement with the assigned reading. There is no single required question.
2. Use the seminar rota to determine which group leads at each meeting. Score each leading student individually as the discussion happens; look for a question that advances discussion, attention to reasons, and an accurate account of the group’s position.
3. While the leading group discusses, the other groups listen, make their own notes, and agree on a disagreement to report. Notes remain with students and are not collected.
4. Listen for relevant reasons and responses to others during whole-class discussion. Record scores individually using the rubric levels. Do not use frequency of speaking as the measure of contribution.

t_ab8b493b9c2f.title: Weekly reading responses
t_ab8b493b9c2f.prompt: Write a response of 400 to 500 words to the reading or topic of the lesson at which this response is due. This is your own work. Weekly reading responses count for 20% of the course grade. Each response is due at the start of the lesson after the one that sets it.
steps: Identify a central claim in the reading or a central issue in the topic, and explain it in your own words.
Explain a reason offered for the claim, or a reason relevant to the issue. Identify any assumption on which the reason depends.
Develop a challenge to the claim or reason, and explain why the challenge matters.
Give your own reasoned judgment, addressing how a defender of the claim or another position on the issue might respond to your challenge.
t_ab8b493b9c2f.answerKey:
1. A strong response identifies a central claim or issue and explains it accurately in the student’s own words. A common mistake is to select a peripheral detail or misstate the position.
2. A strong response connects a relevant reason to the claim or issue and identifies an assumption needed for that connection. A common mistake is to repeat the claim as if it were a reason.
3. A strong response explains a challenge and why it matters to the argument. A common mistake is to state disagreement without explaining its bearing on the claim.
4. A strong response supports a judgment and considers a plausible reply from another position. A common mistake is to dismiss an opposing view without addressing its reasons.

t_53873509f3db.prompt: A valid argument ends in a conclusion you think is false. Is it enough to say you reject a premise because you dislike the conclusion?
followUps: What would you have to add to “I dislike the conclusion” for it to count as a reason for rejecting a particular premise?

Suppose someone argues: “Any act that breaks a promise is wrong. Ben broke a promise to meet Ana so that he could save a stranger’s life. So Ben acted wrongly.” Which premise would you name, and what reason would you give for rejecting it?
Can the falseness of a conclusion count as evidence against the premises? When does that move work, and when is it just stubbornness?

t_c5ac19d03909.prompt: Weston asks us to avoid loaded language and to put our reasons in neutral, concrete words. Compare “Slaughterhouses butcher helpless creatures” with “Slaughterhouses kill animals for food.” Does rewriting the first sentence in neutral words weaken a moral argument, or does it only show what the argument actually claims?
followUps: Which of the two sentences states a reason, and which mainly expresses a feeling about slaughterhouses?
Can a good moral argument include a premise that carries moral feeling, such as “causing needless suffering is terrible,” and still follow Weston’s rules? What would make that premise acceptable?
If the neutral version persuades no one, what has the rewriting shown about the original argument?

t_2200b1b2d7dc.prompt: Consider: “The library should stay open later because many students work during the day and the library is their only quiet study space.” Which statement is the conclusion?

choices.text: Many students work during the day.
The library is their only quiet study space.
Students need a quiet place to study.
The library should stay open later.

t_2200b1b2d7dc.explanation: The recommendation that the library should stay open later is supported by the reasons after “because.” “Many students work during the day” and “The library is their only quiet study space” are stated premises. “Students need a quiet place to study” is a possible additional premise, not the stated conclusion.

t_6c2c253a8099.prompt: Consider: “Leah found the lost wallet, so she ought to return it to its owner.” Which hidden premise would make the conclusion follow from the stated reason?

choices.text: Anyone who finds a lost wallet ought to return it to its owner.
Anyone who returns a lost wallet knows who its owner is.
Anyone who owns a wallet ought to keep it secure.
Anyone who finds a lost wallet is able to identify its owner.

t_6c2c253a8099.explanation: The hidden premise connects finding a lost wallet to the obligation to return it. “Anyone who returns a lost wallet knows who its owner is” concerns knowledge rather than an obligation. “Anyone who owns a wallet ought to keep it secure” concerns the owner’s conduct. “Anyone who finds a lost wallet is able to identify its owner” concerns ability rather than what the finder ought to do.

t_2a77e3cca605.prompt: An argument concludes that a park should remain open. If the argument is valid, the park should remain open.

choices.text: True
False

t_2a77e3cca605.explanation: Validity means that the conclusion must be true if the premises are true. The premises could be false, so validity alone does not establish that the park should remain open.

t_60039b3940c7.prompt: Consider: “Every action that breaks a rule is wrong. Priya broke a rule. Therefore, Priya acted wrongly.” The first premise is false. How should the argument be classified?

choices.text: Invalid but sound
Valid and sound
Valid but unsound
Invalid and unsound

t_60039b3940c7.explanation: The conclusion follows from the premises, so the argument is valid. Its false first premise makes it unsound. “Invalid but sound” is impossible because soundness requires validity. “Valid and sound” overlooks the false premise. “Invalid and unsound” misses that the conclusion follows from the premises.

t_1337cda3c0d0.prompt: Consider: “Only a selfish neighbor would oppose the community garden, so the garden must be built.” Rewrite the argument as numbered premises and a conclusion using neutral, concrete language. Then name one premise that needs defense and explain why.
t_1337cda3c0d0.answer: P1. A community garden would give residents a place to grow food. P2. The city should build a community garden if it would give residents a place to grow food. C. The city should build the community garden. P2 needs defense because the benefit of growing food may not by itself settle whether the garden should be built.
t_1337cda3c0d0.explanation: The original calls opponents “selfish” without giving a reason for building the garden. A faithful revision states the original reason neutrally (some neighbors oppose the garden out of self-interest), shows that it gives no reason to build the garden, and names the premise that would be needed; a benefit like the one above is a new reason and must be marked as added. The proposed benefit is a claim to investigate, not an established fact. Other coherent reconstructions are possible; each should identify a premise and explain why it needs support.

t_3e4dacfec929.prompt: In chapter 2, Rachels draws three consequences from taking cultural relativism seriously. We could not say that another society’s customs are morally inferior to our own. We could decide whether an action is right or wrong simply by consulting our own society’s standards. And the idea of moral progress would be called into doubt. Choose one of the three. Is it a reason to reject cultural relativism, or a cost a relativist can accept?
followUps: Which of the three would a relativist find hardest to accept, and what is your reason?
Suppose a relativist accepts the cost. Has Rachels refuted relativism, or only shown that it is expensive?
If a consequence is unwelcome, does that count as evidence that the theory is false? Why or why not?

t_29e0486a5932.prompt: Rachels suggests that relativism leaves one lesson worth keeping: be wary of treating the preferences of your own culture as a universal standard. Can you keep that caution while rejecting relativism? What would show you that one of your own moral beliefs is a preference of your culture rather than a moral truth?
followUps: Name a belief you hold that you suspect comes mostly from your upbringing. What would you need to find out to test it?
Does the caution itself rest on an objective standard, such as a duty to be fair to others? What follows if it does?
Where does the caution stop? How would you tell it apart from doubting every moral belief you have?

t_b6b160ec3322.prompt: Suppose society A believes that keeping promises to strangers is required, while society B believes it is not required. Which reconstruction uses this disagreement to make the cultural differences argument?

choices.text: 1. A believes the practice is required. 2. B believes it is not. Conclusion: There is no objective truth about the practice.
1. A believes the practice is required. 2. B believes it is not. Conclusion: Both societies follow the same moral code.
1. A believes the practice is required. 2. B believes it is not. Conclusion: A’s belief is objectively correct.
1. A believes the practice is required. 2. B believes it is not. Conclusion: B’s belief is objectively correct.

t_b6b160ec3322.explanation: The cultural differences argument moves from disagreement in belief to a conclusion that there is no objective truth. “Both societies follow the same moral code” contradicts the stated disagreement. “A’s belief is objectively correct” and “B’s belief is objectively correct” each assert an objective answer instead of denying that one exists.

t_141e096a684f.prompt: Suppose two communities disagree about whether a particular medicine is effective. Their disagreement alone does not establish that there is no fact about the medicine’s effectiveness.

choices.text: True
False

t_141e096a684f.explanation: People can disagree even when there is a fact that would make one view mistaken. The disagreement alone does not establish that no such fact exists.

t_d660912f73e2.prompt: Suppose a traveler argues: “Some societies approve of a marriage custom and others condemn it. Therefore, no objective truth exists about whether the custom is right.” Which claim would make that inference valid?

choices.text: Whenever societies disagree about a practice, one society’s view is objectively correct.
Whenever societies disagree about a practice, there is no objective truth about it.
Whenever societies agree about a practice, their shared view is objectively correct.
Whenever societies disagree about a practice, they have different factual beliefs.

t_d660912f73e2.explanation: The missing claim connects disagreement to the absence of objective truth. “One society’s view is objectively correct” implies the opposite conclusion. “Their shared view is objectively correct” concerns agreement, not disagreement. “They have different factual beliefs” does not establish that objective truth is absent.

t_d31500d809a9.prompt: Suppose two societies disagree about whether citizens should be allowed to criticize their rulers. A student says that this disagreement proves there is no objective answer. Explain the mistake, then explain whether exposing it proves that an objective answer exists.
t_d31500d809a9.answer: The student moves from a fact about what societies believe to a claim about whether an objective answer exists. Disagreement alone does not establish that there is no truth: people can disagree when one or both are mistaken. But showing that this argument fails does not prove that an objective answer exists. That conclusion needs its own argument.
t_d31500d809a9.explanation: The key distinction is between disagreement about a question and the existence of a truth about it. Rejecting an invalid inference leaves its conclusion open; it does not establish the opposite conclusion.

t_e8a144ddf153.prompt: Suppose a society’s code excludes women from voting, and a reformer argues that the code should change. Which consequence of cultural relativism is raised by treating right and wrong as determined entirely by that code?

choices.text: The reformer’s proposal changes the code, so it must count as moral progress.
The reformer’s proposal is unpopular, so the code cannot determine its moral status.
The reformer’s proposal departs from the code, so calling it moral progress is doubtful.
The reformer’s proposal comes from within the society, so it must be morally right.

t_e8a144ddf153.explanation: If the existing code is the standard of right and wrong, departure from it cannot straightforwardly be judged an improvement by that standard. “It must count as moral progress” assumes that change is improvement. “The code cannot determine its moral status” does not follow from unpopularity. “It must be morally right” does not follow merely because the proposal comes from within the society.

t_0650276ce56a.prompt: Which statement best captures Mill’s principle of utility?

choices.text: An act is right insofar as it promotes the agent’s happiness.
An act is right insofar as it promotes happiness impartially.
An act is right insofar as it follows an accepted moral rule.
An act is right insofar as it expresses a good motive.

t_0650276ce56a.explanation: Mill judges an act by its tendency to promote happiness, counting everyone affected equally. “An act is right insofar as it promotes the agent’s happiness” overlooks impartiality; “An act is right insofar as it follows an accepted moral rule” makes acceptance the test; and “An act is right insofar as it expresses a good motive” focuses on motive rather than consequences.

t_08cb7e62bb48.prompt: Suppose nearly everyone who has experienced both composing music and eating a favorite dessert decisively prefers composing, even though it brings more discontent. How would Mill’s test classify the pleasures?

choices.text: Composing is higher in quality.
Eating dessert is higher in quality.
Both are equal in quality.
Neither can be compared in quality.

t_08cb7e62bb48.explanation: Mill treats the decisive preference of people acquainted with both pleasures as evidence of higher quality. “Eating dessert is higher in quality” reverses their preference; “Both are equal in quality” ignores it; and “Neither can be compared in quality” rejects the comparison Mill’s test makes.

t_79a7f66a04cb.prompt: Suppose a town must choose between a quiet garden and a busy recreation center. Mill’s principle permits officials to count their own happiness more heavily simply because they make the decision.

choices.text: True
False

t_79a7f66a04cb.explanation: Mill requires impartiality: the happiness of officials and other people affected counts equally. The officials’ role as decision makers gives their happiness no extra weight.

t_43ea5312b2b0.prompt: Suppose a council must choose between repairing a bridge used by 200 residents and improving a plaza used by 20,000 residents. An argument says the bridge will prevent serious injuries, the plaza will provide mild pleasure, and therefore the bridge should be repaired. What further premise does the argument need?

choices.text: Every bridge repair produces more happiness than every plaza improvement.
The preferences of bridge users count more than those of plaza users.
Preventing the injuries outweighs the plaza’s mild pleasures.
Mild pleasures never count toward anyone’s happiness.

t_43ea5312b2b0.explanation: The conclusion needs a comparison of the expected injuries with the pleasures. “Every bridge repair produces more happiness than every plaza improvement” is a sweeping claim the argument does not need; “The preferences of bridge users count more than those of plaza users” conflicts with equal counting; and “Mild pleasures never count toward anyone’s happiness” wrongly excludes those pleasures.

t_e7f455e3c072.prompt: Suppose a hospital can secretly give an innocent patient a dangerous treatment without consent. Assume that, after every consequence is counted, doing so produces more happiness overall than refusing. What must an act utilitarian say? Give the justice or rights objection and assess one utilitarian reply.
t_e7f455e3c072.answer: An act utilitarian must approve the treatment because the case stipulates that it produces more happiness overall. A critic can object that violating the innocent patient’s consent is wrong even when it increases happiness. A utilitarian might appeal to lost trust in hospitals, but that reply changes the stipulated case: all consequences have already been counted. A rule utilitarian might instead defend a general rule requiring consent, though a critic can ask why the rule should be followed when breaking it would produce more happiness.
t_e7f455e3c072.explanation: The stipulated outcome fixes the act-utilitarian verdict. The objection challenges that verdict, while the replies face different costs: counting further consequences denies the stipulation, and a rule-based reply must explain why the rule should hold in a happiness-increasing exception.

t_2781c5513ec2.prompt: Suppose, in a made-up case, a sheriff knows that a mob will riot, killing five people, unless someone is convicted of a crime just committed. The real culprit cannot be found. The sheriff could frame an innocent stranger passing through town, who would be executed, and no one would ever learn the truth. Suppose also that, once every consequence is counted, framing him produces more happiness overall than refusing. Does the case of the framed stranger refute utilitarianism, or only the version that judges each act by its own consequences? Why?
followUps: Which premise of the objection are you challenging: that the verdict is wrong, or that the verdict follows from the principle of utility?
If a rule utilitarian says never to punish the innocent, what happens when someone asks what the rule does in a case where breaking it would produce far more happiness?
If we reply that the lost trust in the courts would make framing him a net loss, have we answered the case as stipulated, or changed it?

t_6cebf902e6c1.prompt: Suppose a city (a made-up case) has money for one project only. A flood wall would protect 300 homes on a riverbank that floods every few years. A new park would give 30,000 residents a pleasant place to walk. Mill says everyone’s happiness counts equally. Does that principle by itself tell the city which to fund, or do you need a further premise about how to weigh severe harm to a few against mild pleasure to many?
followUps: State the further premise you need in one sentence. Where in Mill, chapter 2, or Rachels, chapters 7 and 8, would you find support for it?
Does Mill’s distinction between higher and lower pleasures help here, or does it only complicate the weighing?
Could someone who chooses the park and someone who chooses the wall both accept the principle of utility? What would that say about the principle?

t_a373a4a61e14.prompt: A murderer comes to your door and asks where your friend is hiding. You know. A lie would send him away, and the truth would get your friend killed. Kant holds that you must not lie. Does this verdict count against his theory as a whole, or only against the view that duties admit no exceptions? Why?
followUps: Staying silent or refusing to answer is sometimes offered as a Kantian reply. Does it answer this case, or does it avoid the case you were given?

Kant denies that duties can genuinely conflict. If a Kantian allowed that the duty not to lie and the duty to protect an innocent life can conflict, would the result still be Kant’s theory, or a revision of it?
Which part of the theory does this case press hardest on: the universal law formula, the humanity formula, or the claim that a duty never gives way?

t_1690c82c467d.prompt: Kant says persons have dignity, not a price, and must be treated always as ends and never merely as means. Suppose a hospital has one ventilator and two patients who both need it, and the staff decide by a fair lottery. Does the lottery treat either patient merely as a means? Does it respect both as ends?
followUps: Suppose the staff instead gave the ventilator to the patient who could do more good for society. Would that put a price on the other patient? Why or why not?
What separates choosing between persons when not all can be helped from using a person merely as a means?
Does the humanity formula tell the staff what to do here, or only what they must not do? Does that limit matter for a moral theory?

t_ed450ede488f.prompt: A student wants an extension and proposes this maxim: When I need more time, I will falsely promise to finish my work by tomorrow in order to secure an extension. What is Kant’s strongest reason for rejecting the maxim under the universal law formula?

choices.text: Universal false promises would make instructors generally unhappy.
Universal false promises would make students generally regretful.
Universal false promises would undermine trust in such promises.
Universal false promises would express a desire for more time.

t_ed450ede488f.explanation: If everyone made such false promises, instructors would have reason not to believe them, so the maxim would undermine the practice it relies on. “Universal false promises would make instructors generally unhappy” appeals to consequences rather than the maxim’s self-defeat. “Universal false promises would make students generally regretful” focuses on feelings rather than the test. “Universal false promises would express a desire for more time” does not explain why the maxim fails.

t_5c2ab007a071.prompt: A tailor and a customer agree on the price of a repair. The customer treats the tailor as a means to getting the repair, but this does not by itself mean that the customer treats the tailor merely as a means.

choices.text: True
False

t_5c2ab007a071.explanation: The humanity formula does not forbid all cooperation in which one person helps another achieve an end. An honest agreement can respect the tailor’s ability to choose whether to provide the service.

t_0f358a6bb187.prompt: A researcher tells a volunteer that a survey is anonymous, knowing that the researcher will attach the volunteer’s name to the answers. Why does this deception treat the volunteer merely as a means?

choices.text: It asks the volunteer to help the researcher achieve a goal.
It prevents the volunteer from agreeing to the actual use of the answers.
It makes the researcher’s goal depend on another person’s work.
It places the researcher’s interests alongside the volunteer’s interests.

t_0f358a6bb187.explanation: The false assurance bypasses the volunteer’s ability to decide whether to participate on the real terms. “It asks the volunteer to help the researcher achieve a goal” describes cooperation that can be permissible. “It makes the researcher’s goal depend on another person’s work” is also compatible with consent. “It places the researcher’s interests alongside the volunteer’s interests” does not by itself show disrespect.

t_b9f96aa88626.prompt: Suppose an attacker asks where a stranger is hiding, and you know that a lie will send the attacker away and save the stranger. Which comparison best captures the Kant and Mill positions studied?

choices.text: Kant rejects the lie as contrary to duty; Mill permits it because it prevents grave harm.
Kant permits the lie because it respects the stranger; Mill rejects it because truth builds trust.
Kant and Mill both permit the lie because saving a life is the best outcome.
Kant and Mill both reject the lie because a duty of truthfulness has no exceptions.

t_b9f96aa88626.explanation: On the positions studied, Kant holds that the duty not to lie admits no exceptions, while Mill permits an exception when a lie prevents serious harm. “Kant permits the lie because it respects the stranger; Mill rejects it because truth builds trust” reverses their verdicts. “Kant and Mill both permit the lie because saving a life is the best outcome” gives Kant a consequentialist reason. “Kant and Mill both reject the lie because a duty of truthfulness has no exceptions” gives Mill Kant’s strict view.

t_0f365b00e39f.prompt: Suppose a tenant proposes this maxim: When I want to rent an apartment, I will falsely promise to pay rent in order to obtain the apartment. A student objects that the maxim fails Kant’s universal law test because the landlord will lose money. Explain the mistake and give a reason based on Kant’s test.
t_0f365b00e39f.answer: The objection appeals to a bad result rather than showing that the maxim defeats itself. If everyone made false promises to pay rent when seeking an apartment, landlords would stop relying on those promises. The false promise would then no longer secure the apartment in the way the maxim requires.
t_0f365b00e39f.explanation: Kant’s test asks whether the maxim can be universalized. Here the proposed action depends on landlords trusting a promise that would lose its force if everyone followed the maxim. The landlord’s loss alone does not establish that contradiction.

t_bfc5c4882807.prompt: Is it a defect in an ethical theory if it cannot say what to do in a dilemma, or is it enough that it tells us what kind of person to be? Why?
followUps: Suppose honesty and kindness pull in opposite directions. What would a person of practical wisdom do, and how could you tell from the theory itself, without already knowing what such a person would choose?
Mill and Kant each give a question to ask about an act. Does that make their theories better guides in a dilemma, or only more rigid?

If Aristotle’s aim is a flourishing life, not a decision procedure, is it fair to judge his theory by whether it settles a dilemma? Which of the claims about habituation or the mean would you point to in your answer?

t_3003394ff5ef.prompt: Aristotle says the mean is relative to us, not the arithmetic middle. If ten pounds of food is too much and two too little for a particular person, the trainer will not simply order six, and the wrestler Milo needs more than a beginner. Is this a strength or a weakness of the doctrine of the mean?
followUps: Take courage. Why might the right amount of fear differ for a trained soldier and a novice, and does that make the mean more useful or less?
If the only test for the mean is the judgment of the practically wise, what stops that judgment from being circular or arbitrary?
Aristotle says some acts, such as murder, have no mean at all. Does that rescue the doctrine from the charge of being too flexible, or does it show the doctrine cannot cover all of ethics?

t_f99df130b4c7.prompt: A student says that generosity requires everyone to give away half of their money. How would Aristotle’s doctrine of the mean challenge this claim?

choices.text: The right amount is always halfway between giving nothing and giving everything.
The right amount is whatever the giver happens to enjoy.
The right amount is fixed by the same rule for every person.
The right amount depends on the person and circumstances.

t_f99df130b4c7.explanation: For Aristotle, the mean is relative to the person and situation and is determined by practical wisdom. “The right amount is always halfway between giving nothing and giving everything” treats the mean as an arithmetic average. “The right amount is whatever the giver happens to enjoy” makes preference the standard. “The right amount is fixed by the same rule for every person” ignores differences in circumstances.

t_b761105062a0.prompt: A student becomes honest in Aristotle’s full sense simply by repeatedly telling the truth, even if they never knowingly choose honesty for its own sake.

choices.text: True
False

t_b761105062a0.explanation: Practice helps form virtue, but Aristotle also requires the person to act knowingly, choose the act for its own sake, and act from a firm character. Repetition alone is not enough.

t_e9747390c3e2.prompt: A person is learning to be fair. Which account best describes Aristotle’s view of how they can acquire that virtue?

choices.text: They practice fair actions with guidance until fairness becomes a settled character.
They discover fairness fully formed in their nature and put it into action.
They repeat fair actions until the movements become automatic, whatever they choose.
They learn a definition of fairness and thereby acquire a settled character.

t_e9747390c3e2.explanation: Guided practice can develop a settled disposition to choose fair acts for their own sake. “They discover fairness fully formed in their nature and put it into action” treats virtue as complete by nature. “They repeat fair actions until the movements become automatic, whatever they choose” overlooks knowing choice. “They learn a definition of fairness and thereby acquire a settled character” substitutes knowledge of a definition for habituation.

t_79ef7be0f86b.prompt: A draft says: “Courage always means taking a moderate risk. If two people face the same danger, they must take the same action to be courageous.” Identify the mistake and rewrite the claim using Aristotle’s doctrine of the mean.
t_79ef7be0f86b.answer: The draft treats courage as the same moderate action for everyone. Courage is a mean between cowardice and rashness, but the fitting response depends on the person and circumstances and is determined by practical wisdom.
t_79ef7be0f86b.explanation: Aristotle’s mean is not a fixed midpoint or a uniform amount of risk. A courageous response involves facing fear in the right way for the situation; what that requires can differ between people.

t_05d4c61df03c.prompt: Suppose two colleagues give the same helpful advice. One gives it from a settled concern for others; the other gives it only to impress a supervisor. What does virtue ethics especially add to an assessment of their actions?

choices.text: It asks only which advice produces the greatest total happiness.
It asks only whether giving advice follows a universal moral rule.
It asks what their motives and habits show about their characters.
It asks whether both colleagues performed the same outward action.

t_05d4c61df03c.explanation: Virtue ethics gives particular attention to character, motives, and habits as well as actions. “It asks only which advice produces the greatest total happiness” describes a utilitarian focus. “It asks only whether giving advice follows a universal moral rule” points toward a Kantian test. “It asks whether both colleagues performed the same outward action” leaves out the character difference the case presents.

t_0caaec3f24ec.prompt: In a hypothetical town without a common power, a merchant threatens a rival after being publicly insulted, hoping to restore her standing. Which cause of quarrel best explains the threat?

choices.text: Glory, because she seeks respect
Competition, because she seeks gain
Diffidence, because she fears attack
Self-preservation, because she seeks peace

t_0caaec3f24ec.explanation: The threat responds to an insult and aims to restore standing, so it illustrates glory. Competition concerns gain; diffidence concerns fear for safety; self-preservation motivates seeking peace rather than identifying the concern for reputation.

t_df3d0a583d19.prompt: In a hypothetical community with plentiful food and shelter but no common power, fear of attack could still lead people to fight.

choices.text: True
False

t_df3d0a583d19.explanation: For Hobbes, diffidence can cause conflict even when people do not compete over scarce goods. People may attack because they fear others will strike first.

t_41b24269d3aa.prompt: A student says that Hobbes’s second law of nature requires people to give up their right to everything even when nobody else will do so. Which correction best fits Hobbes’s argument?

choices.text: Keep that right until a sovereign commands everyone to surrender it.
Give up that right only when others are willing to do the same.
Give up that right whenever doing so benefits another person.
Keep that right whenever an agreement limits personal freedom.

t_41b24269d3aa.explanation: Hobbes connects mutual limits on liberty to the pursuit of peace and safety. “Keep that right until a sovereign commands everyone to surrender it” overlooks a law of nature reason can discover before a sovereign exists. “Give up that right whenever doing so benefits another person” omits reciprocity and self-preservation. “Keep that right whenever an agreement limits personal freedom” rejects the mutual limits Hobbes considers necessary for peace.

t_ee73abf2990a.prompt: Suppose two settlements agree to share access to a harbor. Each expects the other to honor the agreement only if breaches carry a penalty. How would Hobbes’s case for a sovereign address their problem?

choices.text: A common power can make the desire for safety unnecessary.
A common power can ensure that neither settlement seeks an advantage.
A common power can replace agreements with natural equality.
A common power can enforce the agreement and make compliance safer.

t_ee73abf2990a.explanation: Enforcement can give each settlement assurance that the other has a reason to keep the agreement. “Make the desire for safety unnecessary” misunderstands self-preservation as a motive Hobbes expects to remove. “Ensure that neither settlement seeks an advantage” assumes enforcement eliminates self-interest. “Replace agreements with natural equality” confuses rough equality with a remedy for insecurity.

t_84190dbb692b.prompt: Suppose a town adopts a rule protecting injured wildlife because residents enjoy seeing animals. Does this example settle whether morality is an agreement among self-interested people? Give one reason for that view and one challenge to it.
t_84190dbb692b.answer: The rule supports the view because an agreement can protect animals when doing so benefits the people who make it. But it leaves open whether people owe protection to an injured animal when nobody benefits from protecting it. The example therefore does not settle the question.
t_84190dbb692b.explanation: The residents’ interests can explain why they agree to the rule. The harder question is whether an agreement based on mutual advantage can also ground duties to beings unable to bargain when the contractors have no interest in protecting them.

t_36b2d779afa8.title: Seminar participation
t_36b2d779afa8.prompt: Seminar participation counts for 10% of the course grade. Attendance at seminars is expected. Read the assigned texts before the seminar, bring them with you, and prepare discussion questions in advance. Participation is assessed individually on preparation and contribution, using the rubric below. How often you speak does not determine your score.

t_f2ded383d3b4.title: Paper defending one theory,
t_f2ded383d3b4.prompt:
Write a 1,200-word paper defending one moral theory: utilitarianism, Kantian ethics, or virtue ethics. Develop your own argument and engage with a serious objection. Use the assigned readings to explain the theory accurately and support your interpretation. This is your own work and counts toward Paper defending one theory, (20% of the course grade). It is due at the start of the class on Social contract theory.

AI tools may be used to brainstorm or check grammar, but not to write any part of submitted work. Add a note at the end explaining how you used them. Follow the university’s academic integrity policy.
steps: Choose one of the three theories and state a clear thesis defending it. Identify a specific moral question or hypothetical case that will help you show what the theory recommends.

Explain the theory’s central principle or account of moral judgment in your own words. Use the relevant assigned reading and identify the chapter, section, or book you discuss. Explain how the theory applies to your chosen question or case.

Give reasons for accepting the theory. Set out the premises that support your thesis, including any important premise that might otherwise remain hidden. Explain why those premises support your conclusion.

Present a serious objection to your defense. Identify the premise or implication the objection challenges, then answer it. Explain why your reply supports your thesis or acknowledge any limit it leaves unresolved.
Conclude by bringing your argument together and explaining what your defense shows. Provide references to the assigned readings you used and add your note on AI use.
t_f2ded383d3b4.answerKey:
1. A strong answer selects utilitarianism, Kantian ethics, or virtue ethics and states a defensible thesis, then introduces a question or hypothetical case suited to testing it. Usual mistakes include merely announcing a preference or choosing a case without explaining its relevance.
2. A strong answer accurately explains the chosen theory using its assigned reading, identifies the relevant chapter, section, or book, and works through what the theory recommends in the case. For example, a defense of Mill might explain impartial concern for happiness and apply it to the affected parties. Usual mistakes include treating utilitarianism as concern only for the agent’s pleasure or attributing an unsupported claim to a text.
3. A strong answer supplies distinct reasons for accepting the theory, makes a significant assumption explicit, and shows how the premises support the thesis. Usual mistakes include repeating the thesis as a premise, relying on an unstated assumption, or describing an attractive outcome without explaining why it supports the theory.
4. A strong answer formulates an objection that targets a specific premise or implication and replies to its actual force. For example, a utilitarian defense might address whether happiness can account for justice, while recognizing the cost of its reply. Usual mistakes include attacking a different theory, presenting a weak caricature, or simply restating the thesis as a reply.
5. A strong answer draws together the defense and its limits, gives identifiable references to the readings used, and includes the required AI-use note. Usual mistakes include introducing a major new argument only in the conclusion or omitting source information.
