f_f882494fdc5c.question: Does the minimum conception of morality tell us what the right answer is in a case like Baby Theresa?
f_f882494fdc5c.answer: No. It sets two requirements: guide your conduct by the best reasons, and give equal weight to the interests of everyone affected. It does not say which act to choose. In the Baby Theresa case it leaves open whether an infant who will never be conscious has interests, and how to weigh them against the interests of other infants. Those questions need further argument.

f_8b9575f4594c.question: Does impartiality mean I may not care more about my family and friends than about strangers?
f_8b9575f4594c.answer: No. Impartiality does not mean treating everyone identically. It means that no one’s interests count for less merely because they are not yours. Whether special duties to family are justified is a question for argument. The minimum conception says only that such a view needs reasons that could persuade someone outside the family, and that a stranger’s interests count as much as anyone else's.

f_875bea0f932c.question: How is seminar participation scored, and what if I am not someone who talks a lot?
f_875bea0f932c.answer: Seminar participation is 10% of the course grade. It is scored as the seminar happens, on two criteria: Preparation, and Contribution and listening. Each criterion is rated at one of four levels: Exemplary, Proficient, Developing or Beginning. Contribution is judged by the quality of your reasons and how well you respond to others, not by how often you speak. Bring the discussion questions you prepared in advance, your copy of the text and your copy of the brief and rubric.

f_a8e9a66ce502.question: What do I need to do after the seminar, before next week's lecture?
f_a8e9a66ce502.answer: Read Anthony Weston, A Rulebook for Arguments, and bring your copy. Your first weekly reading response, on Weston's book, is due at the first meeting of How to argue about ethics. It is your own work, and its rubric is printed with the Weekly reading responses assignment.

f_0c5b443c4ffc.question: If an argument is valid, doesn’t that mean its conclusion is true?
f_0c5b443c4ffc.answer: No. Validity only says that if the premises are true, the conclusion must be true. It says nothing about whether the premises are true. Take: “All acts that cause pain are wrong. Vaccination causes pain. So vaccination is wrong.” The form is valid, but the first premise is false, because causing pain is not enough to make an act wrong. So the argument is valid but unsound. An argument is sound only when it is valid and every premise is true. Most moral disputes turn on whether a premise is true, not on the logic.

f_7e96db1ece2c.question: How do I find a hidden premise?
f_7e96db1ece2c.answer: Ask what must be true for the stated reason to support the conclusion. In “He lied to the committee, so he deserves to be removed,” the missing step is that anyone who lies to the committee deserves to be removed. A hidden premise is not a trick. It is what the conclusion needs in order to follow. Once you write it out, you can ask whether it is true, and that is often where the real disagreement lies.

f_4b434888675d.question: If I replace loaded or vague words with neutral ones, have I made the argument weaker or settled the question?
f_4b434888675d.answer: Neither. Weston’s rules ask for neutral, concrete words and one meaning for each term, so the reason is stated instead of implied. Take “Greedy corporations poison our rivers, so they deserve to be shut down.” “Greedy” attributes a motive without giving a reason, and “poison” needs a concrete account of what is in the water and who is harmed. After you revise, the premises still need support, and the moral question is still open. What changes is that the disagreement is now visible, so it can be argued.

f_e355ca9bdace.question: Isn’t cultural relativism just the fact that cultures have different customs?
f_e355ca9bdace.answer: No. That cultures differ is a claim about what people believe and do, and nobody disputes it. The Greeks and the Callatians show it clearly. Cultural relativism, as Rachels sets it out in chapter 2, goes further. It says that no objective standard could show one society’s code to be better than another’s, and that right and wrong are only matters of what a society’s code holds. The story of Darius supports the first claim directly. The relativist needs a further step to reach the others.

f_241960ca901e.question: The Greeks and the Callatians really do disagree. Why can’t we conclude that there is no objective truth about eating the dead?
f_241960ca901e.answer: The argument needs a hidden premise: if people disagree about whether something is so, there is no objective truth about it. That premise is false. Peoples have disagreed about the shape of the Earth, and the Earth still has a shape. Disagreement alone shows only that people hold different beliefs. There is also a second point. Some moral disagreement comes from shared values combined with different beliefs. Both the Greeks and the Callatians want to honor their dead, and they differ about what honors them.

f_de89adc0cfc6.question: Is there anything worth keeping from relativism, or should we just drop it?
f_de89adc0cfc6.answer: Rachels thinks there is a lesson worth keeping. We should be wary of treating the preferences of our own culture as a universal standard. Many customs that seem natural to us may be matters of local habit, and it is a good discipline to ask whether we have reasons for a judgment beyond familiarity. This caution does not require accepting relativism. You can hold it while still believing that some moral judgments can be better supported than others.

f_ffc511cc2f00.question: Does Mill think we are morally required to choose the higher pleasures?
f_ffc511cc2f00.answer: No. Mill’s claim is about how pleasures are valued. A higher pleasure, one that people who know both kinds decisively prefer, counts for more in the total of happiness than a lower pleasure of the same size. It is not a separate duty. Mill adds this idea of quality to Bentham’s focus on the amount of pleasure.

f_b1eec3e318ce.question: What is the difference between act utilitarianism and rule utilitarianism?
f_b1eec3e318ce.answer: An act utilitarian judges each act by its own consequences. A rule utilitarian judges an act by whether it follows the rules whose general acceptance would produce the most happiness. Suppose a rule such as ‘keep your promises’ tends to produce more happiness when everyone follows it. The rule utilitarian says to follow it, even in a case where breaking it might look better. Each version has costs, and the seminar tests them.

f_4cec67cfa2f3.question: The argument for the flood wall or the park needed a premise I had not stated. Does that mean the utilitarian argument fails?
f_4cec67cfa2f3.answer: No. Almost every argument depends on some unstated premise, and reconstructing the argument is how you find it. In these cases the principle of utility alone does not say how to weigh unlike goods, such as severe harm to a few against mild pleasure to many. So the argument needs an extra premise that makes the weighing explicit. A utilitarian should state that premise and defend it. A critic can challenge it.

f_ebb41500e6c7.question: Do I need to read Mill’s chapter on justice for this lesson?
f_ebb41500e6c7.answer: No. The assigned reading is Mill, chapter 2, and Rachels, chapters 7 and 8. Rachels presents the objection from justice and rights in chapter 8 (to confirm). The lecture only mentions that Mill takes up justice in a later chapter, where he grounds it in utility. You can use Rachels’s account of the objection and replies in your discussion and writing.

f_3d709bd2aed2.question: Does Kant think that acting from duty means I must feel nothing, or must act against my wishes?
f_3d709bd2aed2.answer: No. Acting from duty is about the motive that moves you. You act from duty when the thought that the act is right is what leads you to do it. You may also enjoy doing it. The contrast is with acting merely in accordance with duty, where your act matches what duty requires but you are moved by something else, such as protecting your reputation.

f_34e8e0e9b0c5.question: Is the universal law test just the question ‘what if everyone did that?’
f_34e8e0e9b0c5.answer: Not quite. The test asks whether you could act on your maxim and also will it as a law for everyone. A maxim fails when universal adoption defeats its own purpose. Take the maxim of promising to repay a loan while knowing you cannot. If everyone did this, no one would believe a promise of repayment, and the practice the maxim depends on would collapse. ‘The world would be worse’ is a consequentialist reason, and it is not the reason the test relies on. When you write your maxim, include the situation and the purpose, in the form ‘When I am in…, I will…, in order to…’.

f_3044858bdfc4.question: Does the humanity formula forbid using other people at all?
f_3044858bdfc4.answer: No. The formula forbids treating persons merely as means. We use other people constantly. A rider uses a bus driver to get across town, and the driver agrees to this as part of her job. The rider also treats her as a person with her own aims. The formula is broken when someone is deceived or coerced into serving a purpose they could not share if they knew it. Rachels discusses this idea in chapter 10 (to confirm).

f_bd0b22b214b8.question: Is eudaimonia the same as happiness?
f_bd0b22b214b8.answer: Not quite. Eudaimonia is usually translated as flourishing. For Aristotle it is not a mood or a good afternoon. It is an activity of the soul in accordance with virtue over a whole life. His line that one swallow does not make a spring makes the point: one good day does not make a good life. That is why settled traits of character matter so much to him.

f_e02e7a719593.question: Does the doctrine of the mean say I should be moderate in everything?
f_e02e7a719593.answer: No. The mean is not an arithmetic middle, and it is not the same for everyone. Aristotle’s trainer example shows this: if ten pounds of food is too much and two too little for a particular person, the trainer will not simply order six. In book II, chapter 6, the right response depends on the right time, object, person, aim and manner. Practical wisdom, the judgment of a thoughtful person, fixes it. Courage is a mean between cowardice and rashness, but it does not mean feeling a middling amount of fear.

f_15bb8a36d0bd.question: How is asking ‘what kind of person should I be’ different from asking ‘which act is right’?
f_15bb8a36d0bd.answer: Act-based theories put the test on the act. Mill asks which act produces the most happiness for everyone affected. Kant asks whether the maxim can be willed as a universal law and whether the act treats persons as ends. Aristotle asks what a person of good character would do and what kind of person I am becoming. So he gives more weight to motive, feeling and long-term character. Kant also cares about motive, because only acting from duty gives an act moral worth. Aristotle’s emphasis is on settled character and fitting feeling, not duty alone.
